label: Chapter 1
title: The Aristotelian Proof
tagline: From a cooling cup of coffee to the Unmoved Mover
oneSentence: Because change is real, and change is the actualizing of potential by something already actual, the things that change can exist at any moment only if they are held in being by a hierarchical series of actualizers that must bottom out in a purely actual actualizer — which must be one, unchanging, eternal, immaterial, perfect, good, all-powerful, intelligent and all-knowing, and so is God.
bigPicture:
This is the book’s first and most foundational proof. It starts from the most modest datum imaginable — that things change, that your coffee gets cold — and argues, by way of Aristotle’s distinction between **actuality** and **potentiality**, that nothing could exist even for an instant unless it were being kept in existence, here and now, by a cause that is **pure actuality**: an *unactualized actualizer*, Aristotle’s *Unmoved Mover*. The whole argument turns on the difference between a **linear** (per accidens) series of causes stretched out through time, which Feser happily grants might have no beginning, and a **hierarchical** (per se) series in which every member other than the first has only borrowed, instrumental causal power, which cannot fail to have a genuinely first, self-sufficient source.

The chapter has two stages. **Stage 1** gets you from change to a purely actual actualizer. **Stage 2** shows that anything purely actual must have the classic divine attributes: it must be unique, immutable, eternal, immaterial and incorporeal, perfect, fully good, omnipotent, intelligent, and omniscient. That second stage is Feser’s answer to the old complaint that ‘first cause’ arguments can at best reach some cause or other but never God. The attributes get a fuller defense later in the book (the chapter on the nature of God), but here you already see how they flow from a single idea.

The second half of the chapter is defensive, and it is at least as important as the first. Feser clears away the standard misreadings (that the argument is about a beginning of the universe, that it treats the universe as a whole, that it says ‘everything has a cause’) and then answers philosophical challenges from Hume and Kant and scientific ones drawn from Russell, Newton’s law of inertia, Einstein’s block universe, quantum mechanics and radioactive decay, and Eddington’s ‘two tables’. He also defends the reality of hierarchical causal series and explains why the first mover must be not merely unmoved but *unmovable*.

What sets this proof apart from the other four is where it starts: with **change** and the metaphysics of act and potency. The Neo-Platonic proof starts from composition, the Augustinian from abstract truths, the Thomistic from essence and existence, and the Rationalist from the principle of sufficient reason. But the concepts built here — actualization, hierarchical causation, proportionate causality, first cause as ‘underived’ rather than ‘earliest’ — are the toolkit the whole book relies on. Master this chapter and the rest of the book gets much easier.
objectives: Explain Aristotle’s analysis of change as the actualization of a potential, and show how it answers Parmenides’ claim that change would require something to come from nothing.

State the principle of causality precisely (whatever goes from potential to actual is actualized by something already actual) and explain why it follows from what potentiality is, not just from observed patterns.
Distinguish a linear (per accidens) causal series from a hierarchical (per se) causal series using at least two examples each, and explain why only the hierarchical kind must have a first member.
Explain what ‘first’ means in ‘first cause’ (underived rather than temporally earliest), and why even an infinitely long hierarchical series would still need such a cause.
Reconstruct the move from the changes of everyday objects to the existence of those objects here and now, and from there to a purely actual actualizer.

Derive at least six divine attributes (unity, immutability, eternity, immateriality, perfection, goodness, omnipotence, intelligence, omniscience) from pure actuality, citing the principle of proportionate causality where it is needed.
Answer the ‘What caused God?’ objection and explain why it attacks a straw man.

Answer objections drawn from Hume, Kant, Russell, Newtonian inertia, relativity’s block universe, and quantum mechanics, including the key point that an absence in a mathematical representation of nature is not a representation of absence in nature.
Explain why the first actualizer must be unmovable (purely actual), not merely unmoved, and why ‘every actualizer must itself change’ commits a fallacy of accident.

summary.heading: Stage 1: Change is real, and cannot coherently be denied
summary.plain: Everything around us changes: coffee cools, leaves fall, puddles grow, living things die. An ancient thinker named Parmenides argued that change is impossible, because it would mean something coming out of nothing. The book’s first answer is simple: you can’t even argue that change isn’t real without your thoughts changing as you argue. So the argument starts from something no one can seriously deny.
summary.takeaway: Change cannot coherently be denied, because even doubting it is a change, so the argument’s starting point is as secure as a starting point can be.
summary.body:
Feser opens with four everyday changes, one for each kind Aristotelians recognize: coffee cooling (**qualitative**), a leaf falling (**local**, change of place), a puddle growing in the rain (**quantitative**), and a swatted fly dying (**substantial**). The senses show such changes happen. Even if, as in Descartes or *The Matrix*, your whole life were a dream, your **experiences** would still succeed one another — and that is change.

**Parmenides** argued that change is impossible: the coffee’s coldness doesn’t exist while it is hot, so its becoming cold would be something coming from nothing. Feser gives two replies. First, the view is **self-refuting**: reasoning your way to the conclusion that change is unreal means moving from premise to premise — itself a change. Second, Aristotle showed that change does not in fact require something from nothing.

Why does Feser spend so long on something so obvious? Because step 1 of the formal argument rests on it, and he wants that first premise to be as secure as a premise can be. His strategy is to show that change survives even the most radical doubt. You can doubt your senses, and you can doubt that there is an external world, but you cannot doubt that your own thoughts succeed one another. Note too that ‘change’ here is broad. It covers all four kinds, not just motion through space, and that matters later, because substantial change (the fly dying) already hints that a thing’s very existence involves potentials that can be gained or lost. Finally, Parmenides’ puzzle is productive rather than a mere curiosity. Diagnosing exactly where it goes wrong is what gives us the distinction between actuality and potentiality, which drives the whole proof.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea here is the self-refutation reply, and what exactly it proves.

Try a thought experiment. For ten seconds, sincerely hold the belief that nothing ever changes. Notice what happened. You read the instruction, formed an intention, entertained the belief, and are now reflecting on the attempt: a sequence of mental states, each giving way to the next. To *reach* the conclusion ‘change is unreal’ you must move from premise to premise, and moving is changing. That is why Feser says no one could coherently accept Parmenides’ conclusion. The act of doubting presupposes the thing doubted.

Be precise about how much this proves. It shows that **change in the mind** is undeniable, not yet that the external world changes. Feser is content with that. Later, answering the block-universe objection, he says change existing at least in the mind is all the argument needs to get off the ground. So the Descartes/*Matrix* scenario is no threat. Even a deceived dreamer undergoes a real succession of experiences.

Now look at the structure of Parmenides’ argument:

1. If the coffee becomes cold, coldness comes from what is not.
2. What is not is nothing, and nothing comes from nothing.
3. So the coffee can’t become cold.

The weak point is the hidden assumption in premise 1 that there are only two options, being and sheer nothing. Aristotle’s reply, in the next section, adds a third: **being-in-potency**. Parmenides was right that nothing comes from nothing; he was wrong that change requires it.

**How it feeds the formal argument:** this section secures **step 1** (change is real) and prepares **step 2** (change is the actualization of potential).

**The usual confusion:** people think the argument depends on trusting sense perception, or on scientific observations of motion, and so they imagine a sophisticated physics or skepticism could undercut it. But the starting point is deliberately more basic than any observation. A second confusion is to hear ‘change’ as ‘motion’. For Aristotelians the coffee cooling, the puddle growing and the fly dying are all changes, and all are analyzed the same way.

checks.q: What is Feser’s first reply to Parmenides’ argument that change is impossible?
options: Anyone reasoning to the conclusion that change is unreal is thereby undergoing change
Science has measured change directly
Parmenides misunderstood the physics of heat
Descartes proved that the senses are reliable
checks.explanation: Working through an argument from premises to conclusion is itself a change, so denying change presupposes it. Feser doesn’t rely on the reliability of the senses; he grants they might deceive us.

checks.q: Which kind of change does the swatted fly illustrate?
options: Qualitative
Local
Quantitative
Substantial
checks.explanation: A living thing gives way to dead matter, so one kind of substance is replaced by another. Cooling coffee is qualitative, the falling leaf local, the growing puddle quantitative.

checks.q: Why doesn’t the dream or *Matrix* scenario threaten the premise that change is real?
options: Dreams are too rare to matter
Even a dreamer’s experiences succeed one another, and that succession is change
Simulations must obey the laws of physics
Feser proves that we are not dreaming
checks.explanation: Feser grants the far-fetched scenario for argument’s sake; change in one’s thoughts and experiences would still occur.

summary.heading: Aristotle’s answer: actuality and potentiality
summary.plain: Aristotle’s fix for Parmenides: before hot coffee is cold, its coldness isn’t nothing. It’s a real ‘can be’ in the coffee. Coffee can get cold, but it can’t turn into a chicken. Philosophers call what a thing actually is its ‘actuality’, and what it can become its ‘potentiality’. Change is just a ‘can be’ becoming an ‘is’.
summary.takeaway: A potential is a real, specific capacity, not nothing, so change is the actualizing of a potential rather than something coming from nothing.
summary.body:
While the coffee is hot, its coldness is not **actual**, but it isn’t nothing either: it is there **potentially**. The coffee can cool, stain the rug, or wake you up; it cannot power an engine, turn into chicken soup, or become a live chicken. That it has some potentials and lacks others shows potentiality is something real and determinate, between full actuality and sheer nothing. So change is **the actualization of a potential** — not something from nothing, because the potential was never nothing.

Notice where a thing’s potentials come from: they are rooted in what the thing actually is. The coffee can cool because it is actually a hot liquid, and it can wake you up because it actually contains caffeine. A rubber ball, being what it actually is, can be squashed and bounce back. An ice cube can melt. Neither can do what the other does. So potentiality isn’t a free-floating ‘anything goes’. Each thing carries a definite range of potentials, fixed by its actual nature, and lacks others entirely.

Aristotle doesn’t reject Parmenides’ principle that nothing comes from nothing; he accepts it and refines the analysis of change so that it no longer seems to violate that principle. Feser calls this pattern typical of the chapter. The ‘semitechnical jargon’ of act and potency doesn’t contradict common sense; it lets us follow common sense out to its implications. Once we have the distinction, change becomes intelligible. The coffee persists through the change and goes from being potentially cold to being actually cold.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea is the claim that a potential is ‘not nothing’. It sounds like a verbal trick until you lay out three cases side by side:

- **Actual coldness**: the coffee is cold.
- **Potential coldness**: the coffee is hot but *can* become cold.
- **No potential at all**: the coffee cannot become a live chicken, however long you wait.

The difference between the second and third cases is real. It is a fact about the coffee, not about our imagination, that the coffee has one capacity and lacks the other. That fact is what Aristotle calls potentiality. It sits between full actuality and sheer nothingness.

Take an acorn as a worked example. It is *actually* an acorn: small, brown, hard. It is *potentially* an oak. It is not potentially a dog, a violin, or a sonnet. When it grows into an oak, nothing comes from nothing; a potential it always had is actualized. And its potential to become an oak is grounded in what it actually is. Potency is always the potency *of* some actual thing.

**A crucial nuance:** potentiality is not the same as logical or imaginative possibility. In a cartoon, coffee could turn into a chicken, and there is no contradiction in the idea. But the coffee has no *potency* for it. When the chapter speaks of potentials, it means real capacities in things.

**How it feeds the formal argument:** this is **step 2** (change is the actualization of a potential). It also sets up **step 4**. Precisely because a potential is not yet actual, it can’t do anything on its own. And it foreshadows the conclusion. At one extreme is the mere potential that can’t act; at the other is **pure actuality**, which has no unrealized potential at all.

**The usual confusion:** people hear ‘potential’ as ‘hypothetical’ or ‘merely imagined’, and then Aristotle’s solution looks like wordplay. It isn’t. Potentials are as real as the chemistry of the coffee. A second confusion is to think Aristotle denies that nothing comes from nothing. He affirms it, and that is why he needs potency.

checks.q: Why does it matter that coffee can cool but cannot become chicken soup?
options: It shows coffee cannot really change at all
It proves the principle of causality directly
It shows a thing’s potentials are specific and real rather than nothing
It shows soup is more actual than coffee
checks.explanation: Having some potentials and lacking others shows potentiality is a determinate feature of the thing. That is why Aristotle can say the coffee’s coldness was ‘not nothing’ before it cooled.

checks.q: Does Aristotle accept Parmenides’ principle that something cannot come from nothing?
options: No, he rejects it as the source of Parmenides’ error
Yes. He agrees, and shows that change doesn’t require something to come from nothing
Only for substantial change
Only for material things
checks.explanation: Aristotle keeps the principle and denies the hidden assumption that what doesn’t actually exist is simply nothing.

summary.heading: Change requires a changer: the principle of causality
summary.plain: A ‘can be’ can’t turn itself into an ‘is’; something that already ‘is’ has to do it, as the cool air in the room cools the coffee. This is called the principle of causality. Notice that it doesn’t say ‘everything has a cause’. It says only that whatever goes from ‘can be’ to ‘is’ needs something to make that happen.
summary.takeaway: A mere potential can’t make itself actual, so whatever goes from potential to actual needs something already actual to actualize it.
summary.body:
Every change has something that brings it about: the cool air chills the coffee; your wrist drives the swatter. But this isn’t just a generalization from examples; it **follows from what change is**. The coffee’s potential coldness is merely potential, and what is merely potential can’t do anything — only what is actual acts. So a potential can’t actualize itself; something already actual (the cool air, ice cubes) must do it. This is the **principle of causality**: no potential is actualized except by something already actual. Note its scope: it concerns what **goes from potential to actual**, not ‘everything’.

Laid out step by step, the reasoning is short:

1. A potential, as such, is not yet actual.
2. Only what is actual can do anything.
3. So a potential cannot actualize itself.
4. So whenever a potential is actualized, something already actual must be doing the actualizing.

That is why Feser insists the principle is not a mere inductive generalization, like ‘all swans are white’, which one black swan could overturn. It follows from what potentiality is. To refute it, a critic can’t just point to a puzzling case. He would have to show a merely potential feature bringing itself into actuality, which is exactly what the definition of potentiality rules out.

Two further points of precision. Feser calls the cause a ‘changer’ colloquially, but ‘actualizer’ is the exact term, because the principle will soon apply where no change over time occurs at all: the desk actualizing the cup’s being three feet up, and ultimately whatever actualizes a thing’s existence at a given moment. And the principle concerns only what goes from potential to actual. It says nothing about something that has no potentials.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea is why this principle is necessary rather than a well-confirmed rule of thumb.

Compare two claims. ‘Every swan is white’ is learned by observing swans, and it could turn out false: the first black swan refutes it. ‘No potential actualizes itself’ is also first noticed in experience (the air cooling the coffee), but its truth doesn’t rest on counting instances. It rests on what a potential *is*.

Try to describe a counterexample in detail. The coffee’s potential coldness would have to *do* something, namely bring about actual coldness. But to do anything, it would already have to be actual coldness, in which case the coffee would already be cold, which is just what it isn’t. The supposed counterexample dissolves into a contradiction. That is Feser’s point when he says potential coldness ‘can hardly do anything’ precisely because it is merely potential.

**Nuances Feser adds:**

- The principle does **not** say every actualizer is itself changing. That is a separate question, and the chapter will argue that a first actualizer need not change at all.
- It does **not** say the actualizer comes earlier in time. The desk actualizes the cup’s height *now*, and the sustaining causes of existence act *at the same moment* as their effects.
- It is not ‘everything has a cause’. Only what passes from potency to act needs an actualizer. The difference is decisive against ‘What caused God?’

**How it feeds the formal argument:** this is **step 4**, with **step 5** following from steps 2 and 4. Later the same principle is applied to a thing’s *existence* at a moment (**steps 7–8**), and it is the target of the Hume, Kant, Russell, inertia and quantum objections. Almost every objection in the chapter is, at bottom, an attack on step 4 or on its scope.

**The usual confusion:** people equate the principle of causality with determinism (‘every event is fixed by prior events’) or with ‘everything that exists has a cause’. It is neither. It requires only that the effect be brought about by something actual, not that it be necessitated, and it applies only to what has potentials.

checks.q: Why, according to Feser, is the principle of causality more than a generalization from examples?
options: It has been confirmed by every physics experiment
Aristotle observed it without exception
It is true by the dictionary definition of ‘cause’
It follows from what potentiality is: what is merely potential can’t do anything
checks.explanation: Feser grounds the principle in the nature of potency. Only the actual can act, so no potential can actualize itself. Observation confirms it but isn’t its foundation.

checks.q: Which statement is the principle of causality as Feser formulates it?
options: Whatever goes from potential to actual is actualized by something already actual
Every event is determined by earlier events
Everything that exists has a cause
Whatever begins to exist has a cause
checks.explanation: The principle concerns transitions from potency to act. The other options are, respectively, determinism, the straw man behind ‘What caused God?’, and the kalām argument’s premise.

summary.heading: Linear series stretching back in time
summary.plain: Causes often come in chains stretching back in time: you pressed the button, the air conditioner came on, the air cooled, the coffee cooled. Surprisingly, the book admits that such a chain could go back forever, with no first moment and no beginning of the universe. The argument doesn’t need a beginning, so debates about the Big Bang don’t affect it.
summary.takeaway: Feser grants that a series of causes stretching back through time might have no beginning; the argument doesn’t depend on the universe having a start.
summary.body:
Often a changer is itself being changed: the air’s coolness was actualized by the air conditioner; your wrist’s motion by firing neurons. Feser is careful not to claim that every changer must itself be changing — that doesn’t follow and isn’t true. The point is conditional: *if* a cause is changing, its change needs a cause.

So we get series: coffee ← air ← air conditioner ← your pressing the button; fly ← swatter ← wrist ← neurons ← irritation at the buzzing. These run **backward in time**, in a **linear** way. Feser then grants, for argument’s sake, that such a series might be **infinite**, with no first moment — as Aristotle himself believed. Many think the Big Bang disproves that; some physicists speculate about earlier or parallel universes stretching back forever. Feser finds the speculation dubious but says it **doesn’t matter**: the argument works even for a beginningless universe or multiverse.

Why concede an infinite past? Partly for strategy. Whether the Big Bang was an absolute beginning is a disputed empirical question, and Feser doesn’t want a proof of God to depend on how that dispute turns out. (Historically, Aquinas also held that reason alone can’t demonstrate that the world had a beginning; this is a course note, not a claim from this chapter.) But mainly the concession reflects what a linear series is. Once each member exists, it acts on its own power relative to the others. The air conditioner keeps running after you leave, and nothing about its present activity requires that you still be acting. So nothing in the series itself demands a first member, and Feser has no need to deny that it might stretch back without end. The argument’s real work is done elsewhere, by a kind of series that operates at every moment.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea here is why conceding an infinite past costs the argument nothing, and why Feser is careful about the claim ‘every changer is itself changing’.

Take the second point first. Feser explicitly says he is *not* claiming that everything that causes change must itself be changing. The claim is conditional: *if* a cause is changing, then its change needs a changer. This care matters. If every cause of change had to be changing, then by definition there could be no unchanging first cause, and the argument’s conclusion would be ruled out from the start. By keeping the claim conditional, Feser leaves room for a cause that actualizes without being actualized.

Now the infinite past. Picture a line of dominoes stretching back forever. Each one fell because the one before it hit it. There is no contradiction in each domino having a predecessor. Crucially, once a domino is falling, it doesn’t need the earlier one to keep existing or keep pushing. That is the mark of a linear series: each member, once in place, has its own causal power *relative to the other members*. The family example from the chapter’s footnote works the same way. Al begets Bob, Bob begets Chuck, and Bob can beget whether or not Al is still alive.

**Nuance:** Feser calls the speculation about pre-Big Bang universes and branching multiverses ‘dubious’, but he doesn’t rest anything on rejecting it. He grants it for argument’s sake, as he grants Aristotle’s eternal world.

**How it feeds the formal argument:** notice that no step in the 50-step statement mentions the past or a beginning. **Steps 6–13** are all about what is required ‘at any given moment’. The linear series appears only as a starting point to be set aside.

**The usual confusion:** people assume every cosmological argument is a ‘Big Bang’ or kalām argument (‘whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began’). This one isn’t. A second confusion is to think every infinite regress is vicious. Aristotelians happily allow a beginningless linear series; the vicious regress is the one involving borrowed power, which comes next.

checks.q: Why does Feser say it doesn’t matter whether the Big Bang was the absolute beginning of everything?
options: Because the Big Bang theory has been refuted
Because the argument concerns what sustains things now, not a first moment in time
Because the multiverse has been proven to exist
Because Aristotle already proved the world began
checks.explanation: Feser grants a possibly beginningless universe or multiverse. The argument rests on hierarchical series operating at every moment, not on a first moment.

checks.q: Which claim does Feser explicitly NOT make?
options: Some causes of change are themselves being changed
If a changer is itself changing, its change needs a changer
Every changer must itself be undergoing change
Series of changes often extend backward in time
checks.explanation: He says this doesn’t follow and isn’t true. That keeps room for an unchanging first actualizer.

summary.heading: The hierarchical series: cup, desk, floor, earth
summary.plain: There’s a second kind of chain, one that works all at once. Your cup stays up because the desk holds it right now, the desk because the floor holds it right now, and so on down to the earth. None of the middle items has the holding power on its own; each passes along support it is getting, the way a paintbrush paints only because a painter moves it. Take away the floor and everything above it falls instantly.
summary.takeaway: In a hierarchical series each later member can act only while, and because, earlier members are acting on it. Its causal power is borrowed, like a brush’s power in a painter’s hand.
summary.body:
A second kind of series — the **hierarchical** kind — must have a first member. It is easiest to introduce by looking at a single moment (though simultaneity isn’t what defines it). Your cup is three feet up because the desk holds it *now*; the desk is held *now* by the floor, the floor by the foundation, the foundation by the earth. A lamp hangs from a chain, held by a fixture in the ceiling, held by the walls, all at once. Each case involves actualized potentials (the desk actualizes the cup’s potential to be three feet up) without any passage of time.

What makes such a series hierarchical is the **dependence** of later members on earlier ones. The cup can’t stay up on its own; the desk can’t hold it on its own, since it would fall without the floor. In a sense it is the earth doing all the holding, **through intermediaries** that act like **instruments** — as it is the painter, not the brush, who paints. Contrast the linear case: once you switch on the air conditioner, it keeps cooling even if you leave or drop dead. But if the floor collapses, desk and cup fall **at once**.

Feser remarks that one of his series traces downward to the ground and the other upward to the ceiling. Direction doesn’t matter; dependence does. He also stresses what makes these examples so useful. They show potentials being actualized with no passage of time: the cup is three feet up *because* it is being held, not because of anything that happened earlier. That lets the idea of actualization, first introduced to explain change over time, be applied to what holds at a single moment. Everything that follows depends on that extension, which carries the argument from change to existence.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea is **instrumental** or **derivative** causal power.

Start with Feser’s painter. The brush really does something: it carries paint and makes the strokes. But it contributes no *power of its own* to the painting. Take the painter away and the brush lies still. That is what it means for its causal power to be derived: it acts only insofar as something else is acting through it, right now.

Here is a simple test for telling the two kinds of series apart. Ask: **if the earlier member stopped acting right now, would the later member’s causal activity stop right now?**

- You stop pressing the button. The air conditioner keeps cooling. → Linear.
- The floor stops holding up the desk (it collapses). The desk stops holding up the cup at once. → Hierarchical.
- A hand stops moving a stick. The stick stops pushing the stone. → Hierarchical.

A worked example of your own: in a mechanical watch, the mainspring drives a gear, which drives the next gear, which turns the hands. Each gear turns only while it is being turned. None has any power of its own to move the hands.

**Nuance:** Feser insists that simultaneity is a helpful way *in* to the idea, not its definition. What makes the series hierarchical is the dependence of later members on earlier ones for the very power in question. Note too that intermediate members may have features of their own (the desk is rigid, the chain is strong), but the specific power at issue, holding the cup three feet up, is not theirs independently.

**How it feeds the formal argument:** this is the concept behind **step 11**. A regress of concurrent actualizers of existence is a hierarchical series, and such a series can’t go on without a first member.

**The usual confusion:** people hear ‘hierarchical’ as ‘ranked by importance’ or ‘ordered from big to small’. It means ordered by dependence. A second confusion is to think the desk ‘really’ holds the cup on its own because it is solid. Its solidity matters, but its holding the cup *at that height* depends, moment by moment, on its own being held.

checks.q: Which test best distinguishes a hierarchical series from a linear one?
options: Whether its members are in the same place
Whether it has finitely many members
Whether it involves living things
Whether a later member’s activity would cease at once if an earlier member stopped acting
checks.explanation: In a hierarchical series, later members act only while being acted on (floor collapses → cup falls). In a linear series they carry on (the air conditioner keeps running after you leave).

checks.q: In Feser’s analogy, the desk, floor and walls are to the earth as…
options: the brush is to the painter
the son is to the father
the air conditioner is to you after you’ve left
an effect is to its past cause
checks.explanation: They are instruments through which the earth ‘holds up’ the cup and lamp, as the painter paints through the brush. The father–son relation is Feser’s linear example.

summary.heading: What ‘first’ means
summary.plain: In an all-at-once chain, something has to be the real source of the power that the others are passing along. ‘First’ here doesn’t mean ‘earliest’; it means ‘the one that has the power on its own instead of borrowing it’. Even an infinitely long chain of borrowers would have no power unless there were a lender. A paintbrush with an infinitely long handle still can’t move itself.
summary.takeaway: A ‘first’ cause in a hierarchical series is first because its causal power is underived, not because it comes earliest or heads a finite list.
summary.body:
So a hierarchical series needs a first member, but not ‘first’ in time. Since the intermediaries have no power of their own to hold anything up, the series couldn’t exist unless something could hold them up **without being held up itself**. If they are instruments, something must be using them; if their power is borrowed, something must have it ‘built in’. A first cause here is one whose power is **nonderivative and noninstrumental** — able to actualize without being actualized.

Nor is finitude the point. A paintbrush can’t move itself, and an **infinitely long handle** wouldn’t help; an infinite stack of desks would be as powerless to hold up the cup as one. ‘First’ means **primary** rather than secondary, not ‘the one before the second, third and fourth’. Feser adds that even the earth isn’t truly first in the strict sense — a point that pays off shortly.

It helps to separate three senses of ‘first’:

- **Temporally first**: the earliest event, such as whatever happened at the Big Bang.
- **Numerically first**: the one at the head of a finite queue, the one before the second, third and fourth.
- **Primary**: the source of underived causal power, the one whose power the others borrow.

Feser means only the third. That is why the argument would survive even if a hierarchy were infinitely long. The question is not ‘how many members are there?’ but ‘where does the power come from?’ Notice, too, that Feser’s definition of a first cause, something that can actualize a potential without itself having to be actualized, is already the idea of an uncaused cause, at least with respect to the power in question. The unactualized actualizer is simply this idea applied to the existence of things.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea is why an infinite series of instruments would be exactly as powerless as a single one.

Here is a course analogy that makes the logic vivid. Suppose A borrows $100 from B, B borrows it from C, C from D, and so on. If *everyone* in the chain is only a borrower, if no one actually has the money except by having borrowed it, then no loan ever happens. Making the chain infinitely long doesn’t conjure the money into existence. Somewhere there has to be someone who has it without borrowing it.

Feser’s own images make the same point. A paintbrush with an infinitely long handle still can’t move itself, because wood has no built-in power of motion and adding more wood adds none. An infinite stack of desks can’t hold up the cup any better than one desk; each is powerless on its own, and infinitely many powerless things are still powerless. The need for a first member comes from the **derived character** of the power, not from any problem with infinity.

**Nuance:** Feser doesn’t need to argue that an actual infinity is impossible. He can say ‘even if there could be such a thing’. That concession makes the argument stronger, because it doesn’t depend on contested mathematics.

**Another nuance:** he warns that the earth, which looked like the first member in the cup example, isn’t strictly first. That hint prepares the conclusion that only something with no potentials at all can be first in the strict sense.

**How it feeds the formal argument:** **steps 10–12**. The regress of actualizers either goes on forever or ends in pure act, and step 11 rejects the infinite option because infinitely many borrowers never yield a lender.

**The usual confusion:** ‘If every member is explained by the one before it, then every member is explained.’ Each member’s *passing on* the power is explained, but the power itself never is. Explaining one borrowing by another borrowing, forever, never explains where the money came from.

checks.q: Which sense of ‘first’ is relevant to Feser’s argument?
options: Earliest in time
At the head of a finite queue
Having causal power in a built-in, underived way
Largest or most impressive member
checks.explanation: Feser means ‘primary’ as opposed to ‘secondary’ or derivative, not first in time or first in a count.

checks.q: What does Feser say about an infinite stack of desks?
options: It could hold up the cup, since each desk is held by the next
Without something outside it, it would be as powerless to hold the cup as a single desk
It is impossible, since infinity is contradictory
It would be a linear series
checks.explanation: Each desk lacks the power on its own, and adding more such desks, even infinitely many, supplies none. Feser doesn’t argue that infinity is impossible.

checks.q: A friend says: ‘If every member is held up by the one below, forever, then everything is explained.’ What is missing?
options: Any account of where the holding-up power comes from at all
A beginning in time
A proof that infinity is impossible
A scientific measurement of the forces
checks.explanation: Each member only transmits power it receives, so the infinite chain explains the transmissions but never the source of the power.

summary.heading: Taking stock: the hierarchical series is more fundamental
summary.plain: The book pauses to sum up. Chains through time, the first kind, might go back forever. But every link in such a chain depends, at every moment, on an all-at-once chain, the second kind. So the second kind is the deeper one. Philosophers have Latin names for the two: per accidens (through time) and per se (all at once).
summary.takeaway: Every linear series of causes through time rests on hierarchical series operating at each moment, so the hierarchical kind is the more fundamental.
summary.body:
In a linear series each member has its own causal power (the air stays cool and keeps chilling the coffee for a while even after the air conditioner is off). In a hierarchical series, every member but the first has only **derivative** power. The hierarchical kind is harder to grasp at first, because we must abstract the notion of actualizing a potential from everyday change and apply it where time doesn’t matter. But it is **more fundamental**: every linear series presupposes hierarchical ones, which trace to a first cause — indeed a single one. A footnote gives the scholastic labels: linear = ordered **per accidens**; hierarchical = ordered **per se**.

Why is the hierarchical kind more fundamental? Because every member of a linear series, at every moment it acts, has to exist, and its existence at that moment depends on hierarchical series. Feser’s footnote about Al, Bob and Chuck makes this vivid. Each can beget a son on his own power relative to the others. But none of them could beget, or do anything else, even for an instant, unless the matter of his body were being actualized, here and now, as the matter of a living human body. That is not in Al’s or Bob’s or Chuck’s power. So linear series ride on top of hierarchical ones. Every horizontal link sits on a vertical stack.

The teaching order matters. Feser starts with linear series because they are familiar. Grasping hierarchical series requires abstracting the notion of actualizing a potential from everyday change and applying it where the passage of time isn’t essential. This moves beyond common sense but doesn’t contradict it. And note that ‘accidentally ordered’ doesn’t mean ‘random’. It means the ordering isn’t essential to each member’s present causal activity.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea is the claim that every linear series presupposes hierarchical series. It is easiest to see with a picture.

Draw a horizontal line of events: you press the button → the air conditioner runs → the air cools → the coffee cools. Now, at each point on that line, draw a vertical column hanging downward. At the moment the air conditioner is cooling the air, the air conditioner must exist. Its existing *as an air conditioner* right now depends on its parts holding together as they do, which depends on its materials’ molecular structure, which depends on atoms and particles, all operating at that same moment. The same is true of the air and the coffee. Every link in the horizontal chain sits on top of a vertical stack.

That is why Feser says the linear series is less fundamental. You could, in principle, remove the earlier horizontal links (you could have left the house or died) and the air conditioner would keep running. But you can’t remove the vertical stack under it, even for an instant, without the air conditioner ceasing to exist at all.

**Nuance:** Feser adds that understanding everyday change requires tracing hierarchical series down to a first cause, and then, pointedly, ‘to a single first cause’. That anticipates the unity argument (**steps 15–18**). He also gives the scholastic vocabulary in a footnote: linear = ordered *per accidens* (accidentally), hierarchical = ordered *per se* (essentially).

**How it feeds the formal argument:** this is the conceptual bridge from **step 5** (every change has an actualizer) to **step 6** (every change presupposes a substance) and **step 7** (that substance’s existence at each moment needs actualizing). It is also why **step 13** can say that the occurrence of *any* change presupposes a purely actual actualizer.

**The usual confusion:** thinking the chapter offers two separate arguments, one about the past and one about the present. It offers one. The linear series is there only to be set aside, so that attention shifts to the present-moment dependence that every temporal process presupposes.

checks.q: Why are hierarchical series more fundamental than linear ones?
options: Hierarchical series are always longer
Linear series are illusions
Hierarchical series were discovered first
Every member of a linear series exists, whenever it acts, only through hierarchical series operating at that moment
checks.explanation: Things can change or cause change only if they exist, and their existence at each moment depends on hierarchical series. Hence the Al–Bob–Chuck footnote.

checks.q: What does ‘per accidens’ mean in ‘a series ordered per accidens’?
options: The series happens by chance
The ordering is not essential to each member’s causal activity
The members are accidents rather than substances
The series is irrational
checks.explanation: Each member can act on its own power relative to the others, so the ordering is incidental rather than essential to the causal activity. It doesn’t mean ‘random’.

summary.heading: From change to existence: what keeps the coffee in being right now?
summary.plain: Now the key question. Forget how your coffee was made: what keeps it existing right now? Its water exists only because its molecules are holding together as water, which depends on atoms, which depend on even smaller particles, all at this moment. That is an all-at-once chain of dependence for existence itself, and answers about the past or the future don’t touch it.
summary.takeaway: A thing’s existence right now is itself an actualized potential, so it needs a present actualizer, and that opens a hierarchical series of actualizers of existence.
summary.body:
The pivotal move: coffee can cool only if it **exists**. What makes it exist — not how it was brewed, but what keeps it existing **here and now**?

Take its water. That matter could exist as separate hydrogen and oxygen, yet right now its potential to be *water* is actualized. Why? A past process that combined the gases explains **how the water got here**; the fact that nothing has split it explains **how it might cease to exist**; neither says what keeps it in existence at this instant. ‘Chemical bonding’ just restates the question (the atoms could be bonded otherwise); atomic structure pushes it down to the subatomic particles — why are they arranged thus, now?

This is just like the cup on the desk, except that the **existence** of the thing, not its location, is at stake: the coffee’s existence depends on the water’s, the water’s on an actualized potential of its atoms, theirs on one of their particles. That is a **hierarchical series of actualizers of existence**, and so it must have a first member.

Be clear about the exact question. It is not ‘Why did the water come to be?’, which asks for the cause of its *becoming*, a past event. It is ‘Why is the water existing now?’, which asks for the cause of its *being* at this moment. Each of the two tempting answers answers some other question. Notice also Feser’s precise wording: what is actualized is the matter’s potential to exist *as water, specifically*, rather than as something else. And the reasoning applies, as his recap says, to anything that has the potential either to exist or not to exist, which covers every material thing.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea in the whole chapter is here: why a thing’s mere existence at a moment counts as an actualized potential.

Start from a general pattern. Whenever something has several potentials but only one is realized, we can ask what makes that one actual. The matter now in your glass has more than one potential. It could exist as liquid water, or as separate quantities of hydrogen and oxygen gas (and, given the right conditions, in other forms too). Right now, one of those potentials is actual: it exists *as water*. So we can ask what is actualizing *that* potential at this very moment.

A thought experiment helps. Imagine freezing time at a single instant. The question ‘what caused this?’ in the sense of ‘what came before?’ has no application inside a single instant. But the question ‘what makes this be water rather than separate gases, at this instant?’ still makes perfect sense. That is the question Feser is asking, and it is why the argument doesn’t need time to pass.

Now watch the answers fail:

- ‘A reaction in the past combined the gases.’ That explains how the water **came to be**.
- ‘Nothing has yet split it apart.’ That explains how it **could cease to be**.
- ‘Chemical bonding.’ That **restates** the question: the atoms could be bonded otherwise, so why this way, now?
- ‘Atomic structure.’ That **pushes the question down** to the particles.

**Nuance:** Feser admits his presentation treats water as an aggregate of atoms, and in a footnote he gives the more accurate hylemorphic version (form and matter). The argument works either way.

**How it feeds the formal argument:** this section secures **step 7** (the existence of a substance at any moment presupposes the concurrent actualization of its potential for existence) and so **step 8** (every substance has, at each moment, an actualizer of its existence).

**The usual confusion:** ‘Things just persist by default. Nothing needs to keep them in existence; they continue unless something destroys them.’ That is the second failed answer in disguise. It tells us how the water might stop existing, not what makes its matter be water rather than separate gases right now.

checks.q: According to Feser, which answer explains only how the water might cease to exist, not what keeps it in existence?
options: Nothing has yet come along to separate the hydrogen and oxygen
A past chemical process combined the gases
The atoms’ potential to form water is being actualized now
A purely actual actualizer sustains it
checks.explanation: Pointing out that nothing has broken the water up concerns its possible destruction. A past reaction (B) explains how it came to be. Neither answers the question about the present.

checks.q: Why doesn’t appealing to atomic structure settle the question of what keeps the water in existence?
options: Atoms don’t really exist
Atomic theory is outdated
It pushes the same question down a level: why are the particles arranged this way now?
It concerns only the past
checks.explanation: Every lower level has potentials of its own being actualized, so we get a hierarchical series, not an answer.

summary.heading: The unactualized actualizer
summary.plain: So there must be something at the bottom that keeps everything else in existence without needing anything to keep it in existence. It has no ‘can be’ at all, only ‘is’. Philosophers call this ‘pure actuality’; Aristotle called it the Unmoved Mover. It isn’t something that just happens to have no cause. It’s the kind of thing that couldn’t need one.
summary.takeaway: The first member of the series of actualizers of existence must have no potential at all. It is pure actuality, an unactualized actualizer that could not even in principle need a cause.
summary.body:
The first member must actualize other things’ existence **without its own existence needing actualization**. So it has no potential for existence at all; it is always, already actual — it doesn’t just *have* actuality but **is pure actuality**. It doesn’t merely happen to lack a cause; it couldn’t even in principle need one, since nothing in it could be actualized. It is an **uncaused cause**: Aristotle’s **Unmoved Mover**, or more precisely an **unactualized actualizer**.

The route began not with the universe as a whole but with a cup of coffee. Yet the result applies universally: every material thing — the leaf, the fly, anything with the potential either to exist or not — exists at a moment only if certain potentials are actualized, and so only because an unactualized actualizer is causing it to exist. Retracing the whole route, Feser sums up: from the undeniable fact of change we are led to an Unmoved Mover.

A footnote notes that on Aristotelian **hylemorphism** water isn’t a mere aggregate of atoms (they exist in it only ‘virtually’); its metaphysical constituents are **substantial form** and **prime matter**. The argument can be put in those terms too: matter depends for concrete existence on form and form on matter, so the composite would be an explanatory circle unless something outside it keeps it in being.

Notice the contrast Feser draws between something that merely *happens* to lack a cause and something that *could not* have one. A pebble that no one threw might happen to lack a thrower. Pure actuality lacks a cause necessarily, because there is nothing in it that a cause could actualize. And the notion isn’t smuggled in by assuming God. It is what the hierarchical series itself requires in order to exist at all.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea is the jump from ‘first actualizer of existence’ to **pure actuality**.

Distinguish two ways of relating to actuality. Everything in ordinary experience *has* actuality, and has it mixed with potentiality. The water is actually water but potentially separate gases; the atom is actually bonded this way but potentially otherwise. Feser’s conclusion is that the first actualizer doesn’t merely *have* actuality alongside some potentials. It *is* actuality, with nothing merely potential in it.

Why? Run the thought experiment. Suppose the bottom layer of the hierarchy were some fundamental field or particle. Does it have any potential for existence, any way it could fail to exist or exist otherwise? If so, its existing now is an actualized potential, and by **step 4** it needs an actualizer. Then it isn’t the bottom layer after all. The only thing that can end the regress is something with **no potential for existence needing actualization**, and so no ‘could be otherwise’ that would need a further cause.

**Nuance 1:** strictly, this section argues that the first actualizer has no potential *for existence*. That it has no potential *at all*, so that it is purely actual in every respect, is nailed down in the chapter’s final section, ‘Why an unmovable mover?’, with its three-way dilemma.

**Nuance 2:** the conclusion is universal without starting from a claim about the universe. The argument begins with a cup of coffee, and it applies to every material thing only because every material thing is like the coffee in having potentials.

**Nuance 3:** the hylemorphic footnote. Form and prime matter depend on each other, so the composite would be a vicious explanatory circle unless something outside it actualizes it.

**How it feeds the formal argument:** **steps 12–14**. Either the actualizer is pure act, or the regress ends in pure act; so a purely actual actualizer exists.

**The usual confusion:** hearing ‘uncaused’ as ‘random’ or ‘brute fact’. Pure actuality is uncaused not because it is inexplicable, but because there is nothing in it to be caused. Another confusion is ‘self-caused’. Nothing can cause itself, and Feser never says God does.

checks.q: Why couldn’t the unactualized actualizer have needed a cause, even in principle?
options: It is too powerful to be caused
It has no potential that could be actualized
It existed before time
Causes apply only to material things
checks.explanation: Things need causes because they have potentials to be actualized. What is purely actual has none, so a cause would have nothing to do.

checks.q: Where does Feser’s route to the unactualized actualizer begin?
options: With the universe as a whole
With the Big Bang
With the concept of God
With ordinary individual things like a cup of coffee
checks.explanation: He emphasizes that the argument doesn’t start from the universe as a whole. Its universal scope is a consequence of applying the reasoning to each material thing.

summary.heading: Stage 2: Why call it God? Immutability, eternity, immateriality
summary.plain: Why call this source ‘God’? First, it’s what keeps everything existing every moment. Second, other traits follow from having no ‘can be’ at all. It can’t change. Something that can’t change isn’t in time, so it’s eternal. And since physical stuff can always change, it isn’t physical.
summary.takeaway: Immutability, eternity and immateriality follow almost immediately from pure actuality: no potential means no change, no change means no time, and no change or time means no matter.
summary.body:
Stage 2 argues that the reality of change entails **God**. The unactualized actualizer deserves the name first because it is the ultimate cause of things in the most intimate sense — it **keeps them in existence** at every moment — and second because the traditional divine attributes **follow** from pure actuality. Feser offers a sketch here, promising a full chapter later.

- **Immutable**: with no potential, it cannot go from potential to actual.
- **Eternal**: existing in time entails changeability, so it exists **outside time** altogether, without beginning or end.
- **Immaterial and incorporeal**: being material entails being changeable and temporal, so it has no body of any kind.

Take each inference slowly. **Immutability** is immediate: change just is the actualization of potential, and there is no potential here to actualize. **Eternity** takes one more step. To exist in time is to pass from one moment to the next, with a past no longer actual and a future not yet actual. That passage is a kind of change, or at least the capacity for it. So what cannot change is not in time at all. Eternity here means *timelessness*, not endless duration. **Immateriality** follows because matter as such is changeable (it can be reshaped, moved, broken up) and exists in time. **Incorporeality** follows because having a body means being material.

These are ‘negative’ attributes: they say what the first cause is *not*. But they are powerful. They rule out every physical candidate for the first cause, including a field, energy, or the universe itself, because each of those is changeable and temporal.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest link is between being **in time** and being **changeable**.

Take a stone that has sat untouched in a field for a year. It hasn’t changed in any obvious way. Is it still ‘in time’? Yes, and notice why. It has a past and a future. It could be moved, cracked or weathered. It is *capable* of change even when it isn’t changing. Existing in time means existing through a succession of moments, and moving through that succession is itself a kind of passage from potency to act. That is why **step 22** says that if the purely actual actualizer existed in time, it would be *capable* of change. The claim concerns capability, not whether change actually happens.

So pure actuality is **eternal** in a strong sense: not ‘very old’, not ‘existing at every moment forever’, but existing outside the succession of moments altogether. It neither begins nor ends; it simply is.

Then **matter**. Every material thing, whether water, stone, star or field, can take on different arrangements, states and locations. That is what makes it material. What has no potency can have none of that, so it is immaterial and has no body.

**Nuance:** Feser presents all this as a sketch and devotes a later chapter to a full defense, including attributes (like simplicity and necessity) not mentioned here. He also gives two reasons for calling the cause ‘God’: it is the ultimate cause of things, in the intimate sense of keeping them in being, and it has the defining divine attributes.

**How it feeds the formal argument:** **steps 19–21** (immutability), **22–23** (eternity), **24–25** (immateriality), **26–27** (incorporeality).

**The usual confusions:** (1) ‘Eternal’ = infinitely long time. No: timeless. (2) ‘Immaterial’ = made of some invisible, subtle stuff, like energy. No: energy is physical and changeable. (3) ‘Immutable’ = static, frozen, inert. No: the immutable cause is the source of all activity. It is unchanging because it lacks nothing, not because it does nothing.

checks.q: Why must an immutable cause exist outside time?
options: Because time began at the Big Bang
Because it has existed for infinitely long
Because existing in time entails being capable of change
Because only material things decay
checks.explanation: Step 22: what is in time is capable of change. Pure act isn’t, so it is timeless. The cosmological history of time (A) is irrelevant.

checks.q: Which is the correct understanding of divine eternity in this chapter?
options: Existing outside time altogether, without beginning, end or succession
Existing at every moment of an endless time
Existing before the universe began
Existing for an extremely long time
checks.explanation: Feser’s eternity is timelessness, not everlasting duration within time.

summary.heading: Perfection and goodness
summary.plain: What makes something imperfect is that it’s missing something it should have, like an injured squirrel that can’t run properly. Philosophers call such a lack a ‘privation’. Something with no unfulfilled ‘can be’ lacks nothing, so it is perfect. And since being good, in the broad sense, means fully being what you’re meant to be, it is also completely good.
summary.takeaway: Imperfection and badness are privations, unrealized potentials that a thing’s nature calls for, so what is purely actual is perfect and fully good.
summary.body:
A squirrel hit by a car may be unable to outrun predators; a tree with damaged roots may be unstable or starved of water. Such a defect is a **privation**: the absence of something a thing’s nature requires, a failure to realize an inherent potential. A thing is perfect to the extent that it has realized such potentials and is free of privation, so something purely actual has **maximal perfection**.

Likewise, a thing is **good** to the extent it realizes the potentials of its kind and bad to the extent it fails: a good painter has mastered craftsmanship and composition, while a bad painter hasn’t acquired those skills. A purely actual cause can be deficient in no way, so it is **fully good**.

Two points of precision. First, a privation is not just any absence. A squirrel lacks wings, but that isn’t a defect, because nothing about being a squirrel calls for wings. What it lacks after the accident, the speed its nature needs to escape predators, is a privation. So imperfection is always measured against what a thing’s own nature requires. Second, the ‘goodness’ in play here is the broad, metaphysical sense in which we speak of a good knife, a good eye, a good tree or a good painter: something that fully realizes what it is meant to be. Moral goodness, and questions about God and evil, come in a later chapter. That is why perfection and goodness are derived in almost the same way (steps 28–29 and 30–32). Both are the absence of unrealized potential or privation, and pure actuality has neither. They are not pious extras tacked on to the argument; they follow from the same single idea of being fully actual.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea is treating **goodness** as a matter of actualization at all. It sounds odd at first. Isn’t goodness about morality or preference?

Start with ordinary speech. We call a knife good if it cuts well, an eye good if it sees clearly, a heart good if it pumps blood efficiently, and a painter good if he has mastered craftsmanship and composition. In each case the standard comes from **the kind of thing it is**. A knife is *for* cutting, so a dull knife is a bad knife. That isn’t because we dislike it; it falls short of what a knife is. Badness, in this sense, is a gap between what a thing is and what its nature calls for. A gap like that is an unrealized potential, a **privation**.

Now run a thought experiment. Imagine something that has *no* gap between what it is and what it could be, with no capacity left unrealized and nothing it ought to have but lacks. Such a thing couldn’t be defective in any respect. That is exactly what pure actuality is. So it is not merely good at *something*, the way a painter is good at painting. It is perfect without qualification: **maximal perfection**, and so **fully good**.

**Nuances Feser flags:** privation is measured by a thing’s own nature. A stone’s blindness is no defect, but a dog’s is. And the ‘perfect’ here isn’t the perfection of some limited kind that happens to be fully realized. Pure actuality isn’t a limited kind at all; it has no potentials that could go unrealized.

**How it feeds the formal argument:** **steps 28–29** (perfection) and **30–32** (full goodness). Both rely on **step 20**: pure actuality has no unactualized potential.

**The usual confusions:** (1) People hear ‘perfect’ as ‘morally flawless’ and ‘good’ as ‘nice’. In this context they mean ‘complete’ and ‘fully realized’. (2) People suppose God’s goodness means God measures up to a moral standard outside him. On this account, goodness just *is* fullness of being, so God is the standard, not something measured by it. The chapter on the nature of God develops the moral side.

checks.q: According to Feser, what is a privation?
options: The absence of a feature a thing’s nature requires for completeness
Any absence of any feature whatsoever
A moral wrong committed by a person
One of a thing’s potentials
checks.explanation: A privation is a lack measured against what a thing’s nature calls for. A squirrel lacking wings has no privation; a squirrel unable to run after an accident does.

checks.q: In the chapter’s broad sense of ‘good’, why is a knife that won’t cut a bad knife?
options: Because people dislike dull knives
Because it is made of matter
Because it was produced long ago
Because it fails to realize what a knife’s nature calls for
checks.explanation: Goodness in this sense means realizing the potentials proper to one’s kind, like Feser’s good and bad painters.

summary.heading: Unity
summary.plain: Could there be two such perfect sources? To tell two things apart, one has to have something the other lacks: a different size, place, age or flaw. The source isn’t physical, isn’t in time and lacks nothing, so nothing could tell two of them apart. There can be only one.
summary.takeaway: Nothing could distinguish two purely actual beings, since any difference would imply a lack or potential in one of them, so there is exactly one.
summary.body:
Could there be more than one purely actual cause? Not even in principle. Two things of a kind need some **differentiating** feature. We usually distinguish things by material or temporal features (larger, taller, earlier), but pure actuality is immaterial and eternal. More generally, things of a kind differ by some perfection or privation one has and another lacks (sturdier roots, a missing tail). But pure actuality lacks nothing and is maximally perfect. So nothing could distinguish two such causes: there is exactly **one**, the same unactualized actualizer to which everything owes its existence.

It helps to take this one slowly. The general principle is that if there are two things of the same kind, something must be true of one that isn’t true of the other. Otherwise nothing makes them two rather than one. Ordinarily the difference is easy to find. Two drops of water differ in where they are; two trees differ in height; two squirrels differ in that one has lost its tail. Now try this with two purely actual beings. They can’t differ in place or size, because they are immaterial. They can’t differ in age or in when they exist, because they are eternal. Could one have some perfection the other lacks? Then the one that lacks it would have an unrealized potential and wouldn’t be purely actual after all. So there is nothing left that could make them two. The conclusion Feser draws is striking. It is the very same unactualized actualizer that sustains your coffee, the fallen leaf, the swatted fly and everything else. The hierarchical series behind every existing thing converge on one source.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea is the principle that **two of a kind need a differentiating feature**.

Try a worked example. Two coins come off the same press, one right after the other. They look identical, yet they are two, and we can always find what distinguishes them. They are in different places; one has a scratch the other lacks; one was struck a second earlier. Now imagine stripping away every such difference: same place, same time, same features, same history, same everything. What would make them *two*? Nothing would. You would have described one coin twice.

Feser applies this to pure actuality. The usual differentiators come in two families:

- **Material and temporal features**: size, shape, location, earlier and later. These are unavailable, because pure actuality is immaterial and eternal (steps 23–25).
- **Perfections and privations**: one has what the other lacks. These are unavailable too, because a being that lacks something some other being has would have an unrealized potential, and pure actuality has none.

That exhausts the options, so there cannot be more than one.

**Nuance:** in the formal version (**steps 15–17**), Feser compresses both families into one claim: *any* differentiating feature would require that one of the beings have some unactualized potential. That is the premise a critic must attack to escape the conclusion.

**How it feeds the formal argument:** **steps 15–18** (unity). It also matters downstream. **Step 34** speaks of *the* purely actual actualizer from which all power derives, and **step 39** of *the* cause of all things. Without unity we might have many first causes, each sustaining its own corner of reality.

**The usual confusions:** (1) Unity is sometimes confused with *simplicity*, the claim that God has no parts at all. Simplicity is a separate attribute, defended in the Neo-Platonic chapter and the chapter on God’s nature. (2) People ask whether there might be many gods, each ruling a domain. Any such god would be limited to its domain, and so not purely actual. (Historically, Aristotle himself speculated about a plurality of celestial movers. This is a course note. The unity argument shows why *purely actual* movers can’t be multiplied.)

checks.q: According to Feser, how are two things of the same kind usually told apart?
options: By their names
By material or temporal features, or by some perfection or privation one has and the other lacks
By their causes
Simply by counting them
checks.explanation: Feser lists size, height, and earlier or later existence, and perfections or privations such as sturdier roots or a missing tail. None can apply to pure act.

checks.q: Why can’t two purely actual beings differ by one having a perfection the other lacks?
options: Perfections can’t be counted
Both would then have to be material
The one lacking the perfection would have an unrealized potential, so it wouldn’t be purely actual
Perfections belong only to living things
checks.explanation: Lacking a perfection means having an unactualized potential, which contradicts pure actuality. That is the heart of step 16.

summary.heading: Omnipotence
summary.plain: Power is the ability to make things happen. Every power anything has is ultimately borrowed from this one source, the way a paintbrush’s power comes from the painter. So the source has all power; the traditional word is ‘omnipotent’. Next the book asks whether it can also be called intelligent.
summary.takeaway: Since all actualizing power derives from the purely actual actualizer, it is omnipotent: the source of every power anything has.
summary.body:
To have **power** is to be able to make something happen — to actualize a potential. The cause of all things is not one actual thing among others but pure actuality itself, and the **source of all the actualizing power** anything has. So it has all possible power: it is **omnipotent**. So far, then, it is one, immutable, eternal, immaterial, incorporeal, perfect, omnipotent and fully good. Can we add something **personal**, like intelligence? Yes, but that needs an account of intelligence and a further causal principle.

Why ‘all possible power’ and not just ‘a great deal of power’? Recall the painter and the brush. In a hierarchical series, the first member’s power is exercised through all the others, and whatever the intermediate members can do, they can do only with power they are receiving. Stage 1 showed that everything with potentials, and so every cause we meet, exists and acts only because its potentials are being actualized, here and now, by a series that ends in pure actuality. So every power anything has is ultimately derived from that source. And the source is not one limited actual thing among others, with a fixed quantity of power, like a very strong engine. It is pure actuality, not limited by any potency. Nothing caps it. Note, though, that this doesn’t make ordinary causes fake. The desk really holds up the cup. Its power is real, just not underived. How the source’s causality relates to that of ordinary causes is taken up in the chapter on God’s nature.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest step is from ‘source of all power’ to ‘all possible power’, that is, to omnipotence.

First, pin down the definition. Feser defines **power** as the ability to make something happen, to actualize a potential. That covers every kind of causing: heating, pushing, holding up, bonding, begetting. Physical force and energy are particular ways of making things happen, not the general idea.

Now the reasoning. Stage 1 concluded that every potential that gets actualized is actualized either by the purely actual actualizer directly or through a series that ends in it (**step 34**). So for any power you can name, such as the sun’s power to heat or a magnet’s power to attract, its exercise right now traces back to pure act. The sun can heat only because it exists and has that capacity at this moment, and that depends on the hierarchical series of actualizers of existence. So **all power derives from it** (**step 35**).

A course analogy helps, along with its limit. A power station supplies every appliance in a city: toasters, trains, hospitals. In a sense all the electrical power in the city is the station’s. But a power station has a finite capacity. Pure actuality is not a store of power that could run low. It is actuality without the limitation that potency brings. So being the source of all power, in its case, is having every power there could be (**step 36**).

**Nuance:** secondary causes are real. The desk really holds the cup, and the cool air really chills the coffee. Their power is *derived*, not fake. This is the picture of instrumental causality from the cup-and-desk example.

**How it feeds the formal argument:** **steps 33–37**.

**The usual confusions:** (1) ‘Omnipotence means being able to do anything, even square circles.’ That isn’t the claim. Power is the ability to actualize potentials, and a contradiction isn’t anyone’s potential. The chapter on God’s nature addresses this. (2) ‘If all power comes from God, then creatures do nothing.’ No. The brush really paints, and it paints *because* the painter moves it. Derivative causation is genuine causation.

checks.q: What does Feser mean by ‘power’ in the omnipotence argument?
options: Physical force, as measured in newtons
The authority to command obedience
The ability to do anything imaginable, including contradictions
The ability to make something happen, that is, to actualize some potential
checks.explanation: Step 33: to have power is to be able to actualize potentials. Force and energy are particular cases.

checks.q: Which premise carries Stage 1’s result into the omnipotence argument?
options: Step 34: every actualized potential is actualized by the purely actual actualizer or by a series ending in it
Step 2: change is the actualization of a potential
Step 22: whatever is in time can change
Step 46: the definition of omniscience
checks.explanation: Step 34 restates the upshot of the regress argument, so that all power traces to pure act (step 35).

summary.heading: What intelligence is
summary.plain: What is intelligence at its root? It’s the ability to grasp general ideas, like the idea of ‘triangle’, which covers every possible triangle, and then to combine them into thoughts and reason with them. Having the idea of a triangle means having a triangle’s pattern in your mind without your mind being a triangle. That is what makes minds special.
summary.takeaway: The heart of intelligence is grasping universal forms: having the form of a thing without being that kind of thing.
summary.body:
Traditionally, intelligence involves three capacities: (1) grasping **universal concepts** (the concept *man*, applying to every possible man, not just actual ones); (2) combining them into **thoughts** (all men are mortal); and (3) **reasoning** from thought to thought (so Socrates is mortal). The first is fundamental, since thoughts and inferences are built from concepts.

To have a concept is to have in mind the same **form or pattern** that exists in things. Realized in matter, the form of triangle yields an individual triangle; grasped by a mind, it is had in a universal way, abstracted from all particulars. That is the essence of intellect: **having the form of a thing without being that kind of thing**. A material triangle is triangular; you think triangularity without becoming a triangle.

Why does Feser single out grasping concepts as the most basic capacity? Because thoughts are built from concepts, and reasoning is built from thoughts. Without concepts there is nothing to combine or reason with. Notice what makes a concept special: it is **universal**. Your concept of *man* doesn’t apply only to the men you’ve met, or to men who exist now. It covers every man who has existed or could exist. No picture can do that, because every picture is of some particular man, tall or short, young or old. This is the key contrast. A material triangle has triangularity by *being* a triangle. Your mind has triangularity without *being* one. So there are two ways for a form to exist: concretely, in individual things, and abstractly or universally, in an intellect. That contrast does the heavy lifting in the next two sections.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea is that **the same form** exists in things and in the mind that understands them.

Try this thought experiment. Picture a triangle. Your mental image has some particular size, a particular shape (probably roughly equilateral) and perhaps a color. Now ask: does your *concept* of triangle have a particular size? No. It covers huge and tiny triangles, right-angled and obtuse, triangles drawn in ink and triangles in no material at all. So the concept isn’t the image. It is your grasp of the very pattern all triangles share, a closed plane figure with three straight sides. When you understand that, the pattern is ‘in’ your mind in a universal way. It is the same pattern that is in each drawn triangle, but there it is realized in a particular bit of matter.

That is what Feser means by the essence of intellectual activity: **having the form of a thing without being that kind of thing**. The drawn triangle has the form by being a triangle; you have it without becoming triangular.

**Nuances:**

- Feser describes intelligence ‘as traditionally understood’ in three capacities: concepts, complete thoughts, reasoning. Grasping concepts is the foundation.
- The universality of concepts matters. The concept *man* applies to all *possible* men, not just actual ones. This will matter when he argues that the cause of *every possible* thing must have the forms of things universally.

**How it feeds the formal argument:** **step 41** (forms exist either concretely in things or abstractly in an intellect) and **steps 43–44** (so, since they can’t be in pure act concretely, it has intellect).

**The usual confusions:** (1) Equating intelligence with information-processing speed or problem-solving ability, as in ‘artificial intelligence’. The traditional notion is about grasping universals. (2) Equating intellect with imagination. Imagination deals in particular images, while intellect deals in universal concepts. You can understand a figure with a thousand sides perfectly well even though you can’t picture one distinctly.

checks.q: Which of the three capacities of intellect does Feser call the most fundamental?
options: Reasoning from premises to conclusions
Forming complete thoughts
Grasping abstract or universal concepts
Remembering past experiences
checks.explanation: Thoughts are built from concepts and inferences from thoughts, so concept-grasping comes first. Memory isn’t one of the three.

checks.q: What, according to Feser, is the essence of strictly intellectual activity?
options: Processing information quickly
Having the form or pattern of a thing without being that kind of thing
Forming vivid mental images
Perceiving particular objects through the senses
checks.explanation: A material triangle has triangularity by being a triangle; a mind has it without being one. Images and perception concern particulars.

summary.heading: The principle of proportionate causality: the $20 gift
summary.plain: A cause can’t give what it doesn’t have. If I give you $20, I must have it somehow: in cash, in the bank, or even through a special power to print money. Philosophers call these ways of having something ‘formally’, ‘virtually’ and ‘eminently’. The point is that a cause must contain what is in its effect, though not necessarily in the same form.
summary.takeaway: A cause can’t give what it doesn’t have, so whatever is in an effect must be in its cause, formally, virtually, or eminently.
summary.body:
Alongside the principle of causality stands the **principle of proportionate causality**: whatever is in an effect must somehow be in its cause, though not necessarily in the same way, since a cause can’t give what it doesn’t have.
