- **Horn 3: a part of X that is a mix of act and potency, call it X2.** Then X2’s own potentials need actualizing. By what? Another mixed part? Now we are back in the vicious regress, with no first actualizer.

No option leaves a first actualizer that isn’t purely actual. So if there is a first actualizer at all, and Stage 1 argued that there must be, it is **pure act**, and all the attributes derived in Stage 2 follow.

Now the **incoherence** objection: ‘to actualize is to change.’ Consider why the actualizers we know do change as they act. Your arm is actually *here* and only potentially *there*. To bring the stick *there*, the arm’s own potential to be there must be actualized. The change is required because the arm is **limited**, located, partial and extended. Remove all limitation and the reason for being actualized while acting disappears. So generalizing from limited causes to all causes is a **fallacy of accident**, like inferring that no one over seven feet tall could be president because no president so far has been.

**Nuances:** Feser’s first reply is methodological. If the premises are true and the logic valid, the conclusion is true and therefore coherent. The critic must name a false premise or a bad inference; he can’t just insist that the conclusion is impossible. And ‘purely actual actualizer’ contains no contradiction, unlike ‘immortal mortal’.

**How it feeds the formal argument:** it secures the step from ‘first’ to ‘purely actual’ in **steps 12–14**, and the premise used throughout Stage 2 (**steps 16, 20, 28, 31**) that pure act has no potentials.

**The usual confusion:** reading ‘unmoved mover’ as ‘a mover that happens to be at rest right now’. The argument’s conclusion is a mover that *can’t* be moved.

checks.q: If the supposed first actualizer had a potential that something other than itself actualizes, what follows?
options: It would not really be the first actualizer
It would be self-caused
There would be two gods
Nothing important follows
checks.explanation: The external actualizer, or something beyond it, would then be first. That is horn 1 of Feser’s dilemma.

checks.q: Why does Feser say ‘immortal mortal’ is unlike ‘purely actual actualizer’?
options: Both phrases are self-contradictory
Neither phrase is contradictory
Mortality is a kind of potential
‘Immortal mortal’ is self-contradictory, while ‘something that actualizes without being actualized’ is not
checks.explanation: An immortal mortal would both die and not die. A purely actual actualizer involves no such contradiction.

checks.q: Why, according to Feser, do the actualizers we experience change as they act?
options: Because causation as such requires change
Because they are limited: an arm is actually here and only potentially there
Because of entropy
Because they are alive
checks.explanation: Their limitations explain why they must be actualized while acting. Pure actuality has no such limits, so ‘all causes change’ is a fallacy of accident.

argument.name: The Aristotelian Proof (Feser’s 50-step formal statement, paraphrased)
argument.overview:
The formal argument restates the informal one in two big movements.

**Stage 1 (steps 1–14)** secures the existence of a **purely actual actualizer**. It begins with the reality of change, analyzes change as actualization of potential, applies the principle of causality, and then — the crucial pivot at steps 6–8 — moves from the *changes* a substance undergoes to the substance’s very *existence* at any moment. Existence at a moment requires a concurrent actualizer; if that actualizer is itself a mix of act and potency, a regress of concurrent actualizers begins. Such a regress is a **hierarchical (per se)** series, which cannot go on infinitely, so it must end in something purely actual.

**Stage 2 (steps 15–50)** derives the divine attributes from pure actuality, in blocks: unity (15–18), immutability (19–21), eternity (22–23), immateriality and incorporeality (24–27), perfection (28–29), full goodness (30–32), omnipotence (33–37), and intelligence and omniscience (38–47), the last using the **principle of proportionate causality**. Steps 48–50 gather the results and identify the purely actual cause with God.

Notice what is *not* a premise anywhere: that the universe began, that the universe as a whole needs a cause, or that everything has a cause.

stages.title: Stage 1 — From change to a purely actual actualizer
stages.gist: Change is real and is the actualizing of potential by something actual; a changing thing’s very existence at each moment needs a concurrent actualizer; a regress of such actualizers is hierarchical and must end in pure actuality.

stages.title: Stage 2a — Unity
stages.gist: Two purely actual beings would need a differentiating feature, which would mean an unactualized potential; so there is only one.

stages.title: Stage 2b — Immutability, eternity, immateriality, incorporeality
stages.gist: No potentials means no change; no change means no time; no change or time means no matter and no body.

stages.title: Stage 2c — Perfection and goodness
stages.gist: Imperfection and badness are unrealized potential or privation, which pure actuality cannot have.

stages.title: Stage 2d — Omnipotence
stages.gist: Power is the ability to actualize; all actualization traces to the purely actual actualizer, so all power derives from it.

stages.title: Stage 2e — Intelligence and omniscience
stages.gist: By proportionate causality, the forms of all things it causes must be in it, and they can only be there abstractly, as in an intellect; since the forms of all things are there, nothing escapes its thought.

stages.title: Conclusion — God exists
stages.gist: A single purely actual cause with all these attributes is just what God is; so God exists.

steps.text: Things really do change; change is a genuine feature of the world.
steps.why: Sense experience shows it (the coffee cools, the leaf falls). Even if the senses deceived us, our thoughts and experiences succeed one another, and any attempt to argue that change is unreal is itself a process of moving from premise to conclusion — so denying change presupposes it.

steps.text: To change is for some potential to become actual.
steps.why: Aristotle’s answer to Parmenides: change isn’t something coming from nothing, because what a thing becomes was already there potentially (hot coffee can become cold but not become chicken soup). Change is the actualizing of such real potentials.

steps.text: Therefore potentials really are actualized in the world.
steps.why: Follows directly from 1 and 2: if change is real and change just is actualization of potential, then actualization of potential is real.

steps.text: A potential can be actualized only by something that is already actual (the principle of causality).
steps.why: What is merely potential doesn’t yet exist in act and so can’t do anything, including actualize itself; only what is actual can act. The coffee’s potential coldness can’t make itself actual — the actual coolness of the air or actual ice cubes must do it. Note: this is not ‘everything has a cause’.

steps.text: Therefore every change is caused by something already actual.
steps.why: From 2 and 4: every change is an actualization of potential, and every such actualization requires an already-actual actualizer.

steps.text: Any change presupposes some thing — a substance — that undergoes it.
steps.why: There is no cooling without something that cools; the coffee can only get cold, or be held up, if it exists. Change is always change *of* something.

steps.text: For that substance to exist at any given moment, its potential for existence must be actualized at that very moment.
steps.why: The pivot of the argument. The matter now making up water could exist instead as separate hydrogen and oxygen; that it is water *right now* is an actualized potential. Past causes explain how it got here; the absence of disruptors explains how it might cease; neither explains what keeps it existing now.

steps.text: So every substance has, at each moment it exists, something that actualizes its existence.
steps.why: From 4 and 7: an actualized potential for existence needs a concurrently acting actualizer (call it A).

steps.text: At the moment A actualizes the substance, A’s own existence requires either (a) that A’s potential for existence is itself being actualized at that moment, or (b) that A is purely actual.
steps.why: An exhaustive disjunction: either A is a mix of potential and actual (and so, by 4 and 7, needs its own existence actualized), or it has no potential for existence at all.

steps.text: If option (a) holds, there is a regress of simultaneous actualizers that either goes on infinitely or ends in a purely actual actualizer.
steps.why: Whatever actualizes A is, in turn, either a mix of act and potency (continuing the regress) or pure act (ending it). Those are the only options — like the water depending on atoms depending on subatomic particles, and so on.

steps.text: Such a regress of concurrent actualizers would be a hierarchical causal series, and a hierarchical series cannot regress infinitely.
steps.why: Each member has only derived, instrumental power to actualize — like the desk that holds the cup only because the floor holds the desk. Borrowed power needs a source that has it unborrowed; an infinite series of instruments is as powerless as one (the infinitely long brush handle, mirror images with no face). Without a first member we just pass the explanatory buck forever.

steps.text: So either A is itself purely actual, or a purely actual actualizer ends the regress that starts with whatever actualizes A.
steps.why: From 9, 10 and 11: option (b) gives a purely actual A directly; option (a) gives a regress that, since it can’t be infinite, must end in pure actuality.

steps.text: So the occurrence of any change, and so the existence of any changing substance at any moment, presupposes a purely actual actualizer.
steps.why: From 6, 8 and 12: every change requires a changing substance, whose existence right now requires an actualizer, which leads to pure act either immediately or at the end of a finite hierarchical series.

steps.text: Therefore a purely actual actualizer exists.
steps.why: From 3 and 13: change really does occur (so the presupposition is met), so what it presupposes exists. This ends Stage 1: an unactualized actualizer — Aristotle’s Unmoved Mover.

steps.text: For there to be more than one purely actual actualizer, some differentiating feature would have to belong to one and not the others.
steps.why: Two or more things of a kind are distinct only if something distinguishes them — size, location, time, or some perfection or privation one has and another lacks.

steps.text: But a differentiating feature could exist only if a purely actual actualizer had some unactualized potential — and being purely actual, it has none.
steps.why: Material and temporal differences are ruled out (pure act is immaterial and eternal), and differences of perfection or privation require one to lack some actuality the other has — i.e., to have an unrealized potential.

steps.text: So there can be no differentiating feature, and hence no way for there to be more than one purely actual actualizer.
steps.why: From 15 and 16.

steps.text: So there is exactly one purely actual actualizer.
steps.why: From 14 and 17: at least one exists, and there cannot be more than one. The attribute of unity — the same single cause sustains everything.

steps.text: To be capable of change, the purely actual actualizer would need potentials that could be actualized.
steps.why: Change just is the actualization of potential (step 2).

steps.text: But because it is purely actual, it has no such potentials.
steps.why: That is what ‘purely actual’ means: no unrealized potential whatsoever.

steps.text: So it is immutable — incapable of change.
steps.why: From 19 and 20.

steps.text: If the purely actual actualizer existed in time, it would be capable of change — which it is not.
steps.why: Existing in time entails changeability (moving from one moment to the next, having a before and after); step 21 rules changeability out.

steps.text: So it is eternal, existing outside time altogether.
steps.why: From 21 and 22. ‘Eternal’ here means timeless — without beginning, end, or succession — not merely everlasting.

steps.text: If the purely actual actualizer were material, it would be changeable and in time — which it is not.
steps.why: Being material entails being changeable and temporal; steps 21 and 23 exclude both.

steps.text: So it is immaterial.
steps.why: From 21, 23 and 24.

steps.text: If it were corporeal (had a body), it would be material — which it is not.
steps.why: Having a body entails being material.

steps.text: So it is incorporeal.
steps.why: From 25 and 26.

steps.text: If the purely actual actualizer were imperfect in any respect, it would have some unactualized potential — which it does not.
steps.why: Imperfection is a privation: failing to realize a potential proper to one’s nature (the injured squirrel, the tree with damaged roots).

steps.text: So it is perfect.
steps.why: From 20 and 28.

steps.text: To be less than fully good is to have a privation — to fail to actualize some feature proper to oneself.
steps.why: A thing is good insofar as it realizes the potentials of its kind and bad insofar as it doesn’t (the good vs. the bad painter).

steps.text: Being purely actual, the purely actual actualizer can have no privation.
steps.why: A privation is an unactualized potential, and it has none.

steps.text: So it is fully good.
steps.why: From 30 and 31.

steps.text: Having power means being able to actualize potentials.
steps.why: Power is just the ability to make something happen, i.e., to actualize a potential.

steps.text: Every potential that gets actualized is actualized either by the purely actual actualizer directly or by a series of actualizers that ends in it.
steps.why: This is the upshot of Stage 1: every actualizer is either pure act or depends, here and now, on a hierarchical series terminating in pure act — and there is only one such (step 18).

steps.text: So all power derives from the purely actual actualizer.
steps.why: From 33 and 34: all actualizing traces back to it, so every power anything has is derived from it.

steps.text: To be the source from which all power derives is to be omnipotent.
steps.why: A being that is the source of every possible actualizing power, and is pure actuality itself rather than one actual thing among others, has all power.

steps.text: So it is omnipotent.
steps.why: From 35 and 36.

steps.text: Whatever is in an effect is in its cause in some way — formally, virtually, or eminently (the principle of proportionate causality).
steps.why: A cause can’t give what it doesn’t have. The $20 example: I may have the bill in hand (formally), have access to it via the bank (virtually), or have the power to print twenties (eminently).

steps.text: The purely actual actualizer is the cause of all things.
steps.why: From Stage 1 and step 18: it is what actualizes the existence of everything that exists.

steps.text: So the forms or patterns found in all the things it causes must somehow be in it.
steps.why: From 38 and 39: to cause a thing is to cause something of a definite kind (a stone, not a tree), so the cause must possess those forms in some way.

steps.text: Forms can exist in one of two ways: concretely, as in individual things, or abstractly, as in the thoughts of an intellect.
steps.why: A material triangle has triangularity by being a triangle; a mind has it by thinking of triangularity without becoming a triangle.

steps.text: The forms cannot exist in the purely actual actualizer the way they exist in individual things.
steps.why: It is immaterial and one (steps 18, 25); it is not itself a cat or a tree. Also, as the cause of every possible instance of each form, it must have the forms universally, not as this or that particular.

steps.text: So they exist in it abstractly, in the way forms exist in the thoughts of an intellect.
steps.why: From 40, 41 and 42 by elimination.

steps.text: So the purely actual actualizer has intellect — it is intelligent.
steps.why: Having forms abstractly or universally is the core capacity of intellect. And since it also causes the relations among things (all men being mortal, this cat being on this mat), these pre-exist in it as combinations of forms — i.e., as thoughts, like a craftsman’s plans.

steps.text: Since the forms of all things are in this intellect’s thoughts, nothing lies outside the range of those thoughts.
steps.why: It causes everything that exists or could exist, so every form and every combination of forms is in it.

steps.text: For nothing to lie outside the range of something’s thoughts is for that thing to be omniscient.
steps.why: A definition of omniscience.

steps.text: So the purely actual actualizer is omniscient.
steps.why: From 45 and 46.

steps.text: So there exists a purely actual cause of the existence of things that is one, immutable, eternal, immaterial, incorporeal, perfect, fully good, omnipotent, intelligent and omniscient.
For such a cause of things to exist is exactly what it is for God to exist.
steps.why: These are the defining attributes of God as traditionally conceived, and God is, whatever else he is, the ultimate cause of things — here, the cause that keeps them in being at every moment.

steps.text: Therefore God exists.
steps.why: From 48 and 49.

keyTerms.definition: The actualization of a potential: something that was potentially F becomes actually F. Aristotelians distinguish four kinds — qualitative, local (change of place), quantitative, and substantial. Aristotelians often call change in general ‘motion’; ‘mover’ and ‘moved’ correspond to ‘actualizer’ and ‘actualized’.
keyTerms.example: Hot coffee (potentially cold) becomes actually cold.
keyTerms.origin: Greek kinēsis/metabolē, Latin motus. Aristotle (Physics III) defines change as the actualization of what is potential, insofar as it is potential.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Motion in the modern, narrow sense of change of place. For Aristotelians ‘motion’ covers all four kinds of change, not just movement through space.

keyTerms.definition: The way a thing actually is, here and now; its realized features. Only what is actual can do anything or cause anything. Related forms: ‘actual’ (adjective), ‘actualize’ (verb: to make actual) and ‘actualization’ (noun: the making actual).
keyTerms.example: The coffee’s actual heat; the actual coolness of the room’s air.
keyTerms.origin: Greek energeia (‘being-at-work’) and entelecheia (‘being-at-completion’); Latin actus. Aristotle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being ‘real’ in general. Potentials are real too; actuality is realized being, as opposed to a real but unrealized capacity.

keyTerms.definition: A real but unrealized capacity of a thing to be or become some way. It is not nothing — it is a determinate range of what a thing can become, which excludes other possibilities. Related forms: ‘potential’ (as noun or adjective) and ‘potency’ (the traditional synonym).
keyTerms.example: Coffee can become cold or stain the carpet, but cannot become chicken soup or a live chicken.
keyTerms.origin: Greek dynamis (‘power, capacity’); Latin potentia. Aristotle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Logical possibility. Potentials are specific capacities rooted in a thing’s nature (coffee can cool), not everything that is merely conceivable (coffee turning into a chicken).

keyTerms.definition: The ancient argument that change is impossible because it would require something (e.g. coldness) to come from nothing. Aristotle answers it by showing that what comes to be was already present potentially.
keyTerms.example: The coffee’s coldness seems to spring from nothing — but it was there all along as a potential.
keyTerms.origin: Parmenides of Elea (5th century BC), in his poem distinguishing the Way of Truth from the Way of Opinion.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Zeno’s paradoxes. Zeno, Parmenides’ disciple, attacked motion through puzzles about infinite divisibility; Parmenides argued that change would require being to come from non-being.

keyTerms.definition: Qualitative (a quality changes), local (place changes), quantitative (size or amount changes), substantial (one kind of substance becomes another).
keyTerms.example: Coffee cooling; a leaf falling; a puddle growing; a swatted fly dying.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle (Physics, Categories): alteration (alloiōsis), locomotion (phora), growth and diminution (auxēsis/phthisis), generation and corruption (genesis/phthora).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Accidental vs. substantial change. The first three are accidental changes (the same thing persists); only substantial change replaces one kind of thing with another.

keyTerms.definition: No potential can be actualized except by something already actual; whatever goes from potential to actual is caused. It follows from the nature of potentiality, not merely from observed regularities.
keyTerms.example: The coffee’s potential coldness can’t make itself actual; the air’s actual coolness must do it.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian–scholastic; Aquinas’ First Way states it as ‘whatever is moved is moved by another’. Often abbreviated PC.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Everything has a cause’ or the principle of sufficient reason (PSR). PC is restricted to what goes from potential to actual.

keyTerms.definition: Whatever actualizes a potential in something else. It need not itself be changing, but if it is, its own change needs an actualizer.
keyTerms.example: The air conditioner actualizes the air’s potential to be cool.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s ‘mover’ (to kinoun); Feser’s word ‘actualizer’ generalizes it beyond local motion.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A cause that must itself be changing. An actualizer need not change; the rule is only that if it is changing, its change needs a further actualizer.

keyTerms.definition: A series of causes extended through time in which each member has its causal power on its own (relative to the others), so it can go on acting after earlier members are gone. Feser grants that such a series might have no first member. Also called ‘accidentally ordered’ causes.
keyTerms.example: Button → air conditioner → cool air → cold coffee; Al begets Bob, who begets Chuck.
keyTerms.origin: Latin per accidens, ‘incidentally’; series of causes accidentally ordered (Aquinas; Duns Scotus).
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Accidental’ in the sense of ‘by chance’. Here it means the ordering is not essential to each member’s causal activity, not that the series is random.

keyTerms.definition: A series in which every member except the first has its causal power only derivatively, as an instrument, and acts only insofar as it is being acted on by an earlier member here and now. It must have a first member. Also called ‘essentially ordered’ causes.
keyTerms.example: Earth holds up foundation, which holds up floor, which holds up desk, which holds up cup.
keyTerms.origin: Latin per se, ‘through itself’ or ‘essentially’; series of causes essentially ordered (Aquinas; Duns Scotus).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A merely simultaneous series. Simultaneity is a handy way to picture it, but its defining mark is derivative, instrumental causal power.

keyTerms.definition: A cause that has its causal power borrowed from another and exercises it only while that other acts through it. Related forms: ‘instrument’, ‘instrumentally’; ‘derived’ and ‘derivative’ power (opposite: ‘underived’, ‘nonderivative’, ‘inherent’, ‘built-in’).
keyTerms.example: The paintbrush in a painter’s hand; the stick moved by a hand to move a stone.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic causa instrumentalis, contrasted with causa principalis (principal cause).
keyTerms.confuseWith: An unimportant cause. An instrument can be indispensable (no painting without a brush), but it has no power of its own to produce the effect.

keyTerms.definition: A cause with underived, ‘built-in’ causal power — one that can actualize without itself being actualized. ‘First’ means first in rank or in the order of dependence, not earliest in time or ‘number one’ in a finite list.
keyTerms.example: The painter, relative to brush and paint; ultimately, the purely actual actualizer.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s prōton kinoun (‘first mover’); scholastic causa prima.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The temporally first cause (say, whatever triggered the Big Bang). ‘First’ here means ontologically primary: the source of underived power.

keyTerms.definition: That which has no potentiality at all — no capacity to be other than it is — and therefore needs no actualizer. It does not merely have actuality; it is actuality itself. (The traditional scholastic Latin is actus purus.) Adjective phrase: ‘purely actual’.
keyTerms.example: The terminus of every hierarchical series of actualizers of existence.
keyTerms.origin: Latin actus purus; rooted in Aristotle, Metaphysics XII, and developed by Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A very powerful being, or the ‘highest being’ among others. Pure act is not one actual thing among many but actuality without any limiting potential.

keyTerms.definition: Feser’s more precise name for Aristotle’s Unmoved Mover: a cause that actualizes other things without being actualized. The chapter argues it must be unmovable (purely actual), not merely unmoved in fact. Also: ‘unmovable mover’ (one that cannot be moved or actualized, as opposed to one that simply isn’t being moved).
keyTerms.example: What keeps the water (and everything else) in existence at every instant.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s ‘first unmoved mover’ (Physics VIII; Metaphysics XII). ‘Unactualized actualizer’ is Feser’s more precise wording.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A mover that happens not to be moved. The argument needs one that cannot be actualized at all, i.e. one that is unmovable.

keyTerms.definition: A cause of a thing’s continuing existence here and now, as opposed to the cause that originally brought it about. The Aristotelian proof is ultimately about sustaining causes.
keyTerms.example: Not the brewing that made the coffee, but what makes its matter exist as coffee right now.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic causa essendi (cause of being) vs. causa fiendi (cause of becoming); Aquinas on divine conservation.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The originating cause (causa fiendi). The brewer made the coffee; the sustaining cause is what makes it exist right now.

keyTerms.definition: Aristotle’s analysis of material substances as composites of substantial form (what makes it the kind of thing it is) and prime matter (the pure potential to take on form). Feser’s footnote shows the argument can be restated in these terms. Adjective: ‘hylemorphic’ (also spelled ‘hylomorphism’, ‘hylomorphic’).
keyTerms.example: Water is not a heap of atoms but a substance whose atoms exist in it only ‘virtually’.
keyTerms.origin: Greek hylē (‘matter, wood’) + morphē (‘form, shape’). Aristotle’s analysis of material substance.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Atomism or mechanism, which treats bodies as mere aggregates of particles. Hylemorphism treats a substance as a unity organized by its substantial form.

keyTerms.definition: The absence of a feature a thing’s nature requires for completeness — a failure to realize a potential proper to it. Imperfection and badness are privations. Verb form: to be ‘deprived’ of something one’s nature calls for.
keyTerms.example: A squirrel crippled by a car; a tree with damaged roots.
keyTerms.origin: Greek sterēsis; Latin privatio. Aristotle; later applied to evil by Augustine and Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere negation (absence). A stone’s lack of sight is a negation, since sight isn’t proper to stones; a blind dog’s lack of sight is a privation.

keyTerms.definition: The degree to which a thing has actualized the potentials proper to it and is free of privation. Pure actuality has maximal perfection. Adjective: ‘perfect’. Opposite: ‘imperfect’ or ‘deficient’.
keyTerms.example: A healthy, fully grown oak is more perfect as an oak than a stunted, diseased one.
keyTerms.origin: Latin perfectus, ‘thoroughly made, completed’ (per + facere).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Moral flawlessness only. In the metaphysical sense, perfection is completeness or actuality of any kind.

keyTerms.definition: A thing is good to the extent it realizes the potentials inherent in its kind, bad to the extent it fails to. Pure actuality, lacking nothing, is fully good. Adjective: ‘good’; ‘fully good’ means lacking no perfection proper to it.
keyTerms.example: A good painter has actualized his potential for craftsmanship and composition.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian–Thomistic account of natural goodness: good as the realization of a thing’s nature.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Moral goodness or pleasantness. Here ‘good’ means complete according to its kind: a good painter, a good tree, a good knife.

keyTerms.definition: There can be only one purely actual being, because distinguishing two would require a differentiating feature — which would mean some potential or privation in one of them. Adjectives: ‘one’ or ‘unique’. ‘Unicity’ is sometimes used for the fact that there is only one.
keyTerms.example: Two trees differ in size, location, sturdiness of roots; nothing like that can distinguish two pure acts.
keyTerms.origin: Latin unitas or unicitas; the classical attribute of God’s oneness.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Divine simplicity (having no parts of any kind). Unity means there is only one God; simplicity is defended in the Neo-Platonic chapter and the chapter on God’s nature.

keyTerms.definition: Whatever is in an effect must be in its cause in some way — formally, virtually, or eminently — since a cause cannot give what it doesn’t have.
keyTerms.example: I can give you $20 only if I have it somehow: in my wallet, in my bank account, or via the power to print it.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic maxim, often put as nemo dat quod non habet (‘no one gives what he does not have’). Often abbreviated PPC.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The principle of causality (PC). PC says an actualizer is needed; PPC says what the actualizer must somehow contain.

keyTerms.definition: Three ways a cause can ‘have’ what is in its effect: formally (it has the very same feature), virtually (it has the power to obtain or produce it), eminently (it has it in a higher way, e.g. the power to bring such things into existence in the first place).
keyTerms.example: Twenty in the wallet (formal); twenty in the bank (virtual); authority to print twenties (eminent).
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic Latin formaliter, virtualiter, eminenter; also used by Descartes.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Assuming ‘in the cause’ means ‘in the cause in the same way’. Only the formal mode requires the cause to have the very same feature.

keyTerms.definition: The capacity to grasp universal concepts, combine them into thoughts, and reason from thought to thought. Its essence is having the form of a thing without being that kind of thing. Related forms: ‘intellectual’, ‘intelligence’, ‘intelligent’. In this chapter ‘intelligence’ and ‘intellect’ are used interchangeably.
keyTerms.example: You grasp triangularity without becoming a triangle.
keyTerms.origin: Greek nous; Latin intellectus (often derived from intus legere, ‘to read within’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Imagination or sensation. These deal in particular images; intellect grasps universal concepts (you can understand a 1,000-sided figure though you can’t picture one distinctly).

keyTerms.definition: What makes a thing the kind of thing it is. It can exist concretely in individual things or abstractly in an intellect.
keyTerms.example: The form shared by all triangles, or by all men.
keyTerms.origin: Greek eidos or morphē; Latin forma. Plato and Aristotle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere shape. Form includes shape but means the whole nature or organizing principle that makes a thing the kind of thing it is.

keyTerms.definition: The formal cause is a thing’s nature or form, which grounds how it behaves; the efficient cause is what produces or sustains it.
keyTerms.example: Lead-210’s nature grounds its probability of decay (formal); what generated it and keeps it in being are efficient causes.
keyTerms.origin: Two of Aristotle’s four causes (material, formal, efficient, final).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The modern habit of using ‘cause’ to mean only an efficient cause. Aristotelians count a thing’s nature as a genuine explanatory cause.

keyTerms.definition: Physics’ method of describing only those aspects of nature that can be captured mathematically. This explains its precision but guarantees it omits qualitative and causal features.
keyTerms.example: A metal detector finds only metal; that doesn’t show there’s no wood.
keyTerms.origin: C. B. Martin’s terms; the method traces back to Galileo and Descartes.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A temporary gap that future physics will fill. The omission is built into the method, so no future physics removes it.

keyTerms.definition: Minkowski’s four-dimensional interpretation of relativity, on which past, present and future are equally real, so change is (allegedly) illusory. Feser calls it a picture of actuality without potentiality.
keyTerms.example: Moments of time treated like places on a map, all equally ‘there’.
keyTerms.origin: Hermann Minkowski’s 1908 geometric formulation of special relativity; the view is also called eternalism.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Relativity itself. The block universe is one philosophical interpretation of relativity, which some physicists (e.g. Lee Smolin) reject.

keyTerms.definition: The cause directly producing an effect, which is simultaneous with it as part of the same event (simultaneous need not mean instantaneous).
keyTerms.example: The brick pressing into the glass (not the earlier throw) is the immediate cause of the glass giving way.
keyTerms.origin: Latin immediatus, ‘without an intermediary’. Feser draws on Stephen Mumford and Rani Lill Anjum.
keyTerms.confuseWith: An instantaneous cause. Immediate causes are simultaneous with their effects, but the event can take time.

keyTerms.definition: Treating a merely contingent feature of the cases one has observed as if it were essential to the kind.
keyTerms.example: Every U.S. president has been under seven feet tall, so no one seven feet tall could be president.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle, Sophistical Refutations (fallacia accidentis).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Hasty generalization. They’re close cousins, but the fallacy of accident specifically treats a contingent (accidental) feature as if it were essential.

keyTerms.definition: Arbitrarily exempting one case from a rule applied to others. The ‘What caused God?’ objection accuses the argument of this; the charge fails because the exemption follows from the rule’s own rationale.
keyTerms.example: Things need causes because they have potentials; pure act has none, so it is no arbitrary exception.
keyTerms.origin: Informal fallacy; the name comes from law, where a ‘special plea’ introduced new matter to evade the main issue.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A principled exception. An exception is special pleading only if the rule’s own rationale doesn’t justify it.

keyTerms.definition: Change in some quality of a thing (temperature, color, texture) while the thing itself remains the same kind of thing.
keyTerms.example: The coffee on your desk goes from hot to cold.
keyTerms.origin: Greek alloiōsis (‘alteration’); Aristotle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Substantial change. In qualitative change the coffee is still coffee; only one of its qualities is different.

keyTerms.definition: Change with respect to place or location.
keyTerms.example: A leaf falling from the branch to the ground.
keyTerms.origin: Latin motus localis; Greek phora. Aristotle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Motion in the broad Aristotelian sense, which includes every kind of change.

keyTerms.definition: Change in the size or amount of something.
keyTerms.example: A puddle growing larger as the rain keeps falling.
keyTerms.origin: Greek auxēsis and phthisis (‘growth and diminution’); Aristotle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Qualitative change. Getting bigger is a change of quantity, not of quality.

keyTerms.definition: Change in which one kind of substance ceases and another comes to be, as opposed to a thing merely acquiring new features.
keyTerms.example: A swatted fly: a living organism gives way to dead matter.
keyTerms.origin: Greek genesis and phthora (‘generation and corruption’); Aristotle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Accidental change, in which the same substance persists through the change (coffee cooling).

keyTerms.definition: The principle that makes a material substance the specific kind of thing it is and unifies its matter into one thing.
keyTerms.example: What makes this matter water rather than separate hydrogen and oxygen, in Feser’s hylemorphic footnote.
keyTerms.origin: Latin forma substantialis; Aristotle, developed by the scholastics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Accidental form (a feature like color or temperature that a substance can gain or lose without ceasing to be what it is).

keyTerms.definition: In hylemorphism, the pure potentiality underlying material substances. It has no features of its own and exists concretely only as informed by some substantial form.
keyTerms.example: The ultimate ‘stuff’ that can be water now and separate gases later.
keyTerms.origin: Latin materia prima; Aristotle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Matter in the physicist’s sense (particles, mass-energy), which already has definite properties and so is not pure potential.

keyTerms.definition: A cause that has no cause of its own and, being purely actual, could not have one, since nothing in it needs actualizing.
keyTerms.example: Feser’s description of the unactualized actualizer.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic causa incausata.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A self-caused cause (causa sui). Something causing itself would have to exist before itself, which is incoherent. Pure act is uncaused, not self-caused.

keyTerms.definition: The attribute of being incapable of change, because there is no potential to be actualized. Adjective: ‘immutable’ (unchangeable). Opposite: ‘mutable’ or ‘changeable’.
keyTerms.example: Steps 19–21: pure actuality has no potentials, so it cannot change.
keyTerms.origin: Latin immutabilis, ‘unchangeable’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Inertness or lifelessness. Divine immutability is the fullness of act, not frozen inactivity; a changeless cause can still be the source of all activity.

keyTerms.definition: Existing outside time altogether, without beginning, end or succession, rather than lasting through all times. Adjective: ‘eternal’. Contrast ‘everlasting’ or ‘sempiternal’ (lasting through all time).
keyTerms.example: Steps 22–23: whatever is in time can change, so an immutable cause is timeless.
keyTerms.origin: Latin aeternitas; Boethius’ classic definition is the complete and simultaneous possession of unlimited life.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Everlastingness (existing at every moment of an endless time). Divine eternity means not being in time at all.

keyTerms.definition: Not made of matter and not having a body of any kind. Opposites: ‘material’ and ‘corporeal’ (bodily).
keyTerms.example: Steps 24–27: anything material would be changeable and temporal, so pure act is immaterial and hence bodiless.
keyTerms.origin: Latin in- (‘not’) + materia (‘matter’) or corpus (‘body’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Invisible or made of some subtle stuff like a gas or ‘energy’. Those are still material; immaterial means not material at all.

keyTerms.definition: Having all power: being the source of every actualizing power anything has, and able to actualize any potential. Adjective: ‘omnipotent’ (all-powerful).
keyTerms.example: Steps 33–37: all actualization traces back to the purely actual actualizer.
keyTerms.origin: Latin omnis (‘all’) + potens (‘able, powerful’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The ability to do the logically impossible (make a square circle). Power is the ability to actualize potentials, and contradictions are not potentials of anything.

keyTerms.definition: Knowing everything. Nothing that exists or could exist lies outside the range of the divine intellect’s thoughts. Adjective: ‘omniscient’ (all-knowing).
keyTerms.example: Steps 45–47: the forms of all things are in the thoughts of the cause of all things.
keyTerms.origin: Latin omnis (‘all’) + scientia (‘knowledge’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Knowledge acquired by observation. On this argument God knows things as their cause knows them, the way an artist knows a plan, not by learning from them.

keyTerms.definition: A position that undermines itself, because holding or arguing for it requires the very thing it denies.
keyTerms.example: Arguing that change is unreal requires your mind to move from premise to conclusion, which is a change.
keyTerms.origin: A classic philosophical retort (Greek peritropē, ‘turning around’), used since antiquity against radical skeptics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Circular reasoning. A circular argument assumes its conclusion; a self-refuting one contradicts its own presuppositions.

keyTerms.definition: Rejecting a claim or argument because of facts about the person making it, such as their motives, rather than its merits.
keyTerms.example: Saying the potential-to-actual formulation must be false because theists supposedly adopted it to dodge ‘What caused God?’.
keyTerms.origin: Latin ad hominem, ‘to the person’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Legitimately questioning a witness’s reliability. That can be relevant to testimony, but it is irrelevant to whether an argument’s premises are true and its logic valid.

keyTerms.definition: Inferring that a whole has some property just because each of its parts has it.
keyTerms.example: Arguing that since each brick in a wall is small, the wall must be small. Critics wrongly accuse the Aristotelian proof of this.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle, Sophistical Refutations.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Applying a principle to each member of a class one by one. The Aristotelian argument reasons about each thing individually and never infers a property of the whole from its parts.

keyTerms.definition: Assuming, in the premises, the very conclusion that is in dispute.
keyTerms.example: Sobel’s charge that calling causes ‘instrumental’ already presupposes a first cause; and Feser’s charge that ‘every cause must change’ simply assumes the conclusion that pure act is impossible.
keyTerms.origin: Latin petitio principii, ‘assuming the starting point’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Raising the question’, as in popular usage (‘this begs the question of…’). In logic it names a specific fallacy.

keyTerms.definition: The view that all knowledge derives from sense experience. Hume is its most famous skeptical exponent. A holder of the view is an ‘empiricist’; ‘empirical’ means based on observation.
keyTerms.example: Feser finds it ironic that an empiricist would doubt the principle of causality, which experience confirms at every turn.
keyTerms.origin: Greek empeiria (‘experience’); Locke, Berkeley, Hume.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Science itself. One can accept science fully without accepting the philosophical thesis that only sense experience yields knowledge.

keyTerms.definition: Hume’s argument that since we can conceive of something beginning to exist without a cause, it is possible for something to begin without a cause.
keyTerms.example: Imagining a stone suddenly appearing in an empty space.
keyTerms.origin: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature (Book 1, Part 3).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Conceiving of a thing existing with no cause vs. conceiving of it without also conceiving its cause. Feser says Hume only achieves the second.

keyTerms.definition: A property that consists in a tendency to produce certain effects under certain conditions.
keyTerms.example: Salt’s solubility; the tendency of fundamental particles to affect one another in specific ways (C. B. Martin).
keyTerms.origin: C. B. Martin and other ‘powers’ theorists; it echoes Aristotle’s dynamis.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Categorical property, a property thought of as just ‘being there’ (like shape) with no built-in orientation toward effects.

keyTerms.definition: A body remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted on by an external force.
keyTerms.example: A hockey puck gliding across frictionless ice would keep going forever.
keyTerms.origin: Isaac Newton, Principia (1687), building on Galileo and Descartes.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The claim that motion needs no cause of any kind. At most inertia says uniform motion needs no continuously acting external mover; it says nothing about what sustains the body in existence.

keyTerms.definition: Determinism: every event is necessitated by prior conditions plus laws. Indeterminism: some events are not so necessitated and have only a probability of occurring. Adjectives: ‘deterministic’, ‘indeterministic’.
keyTerms.example: On standard quantum mechanics, when a lead-210 atom decays is indeterministic.
keyTerms.origin: Modern philosophy of science; the term became prominent in the 19th century.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Causation. Feser insists a cause must make its effect intelligible, not necessary. Indeterministic causation is still causation.

keyTerms.definition: The standard interpretation of quantum mechanics, associated with Bohr and Heisenberg, on which a system’s state evolves by the wave equation and ‘collapses’ probabilistically on measurement.
keyTerms.example: Koons notes that even here every transition has causal antecedents: the prior wave state, or the prior state plus the observation.
keyTerms.origin: Niels Bohr, Werner Heisenberg and colleagues, Copenhagen, 1920s.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The claim that quantum events are uncaused. Copenhagen is indeterministic, but it still assigns causal antecedents to transitions.

keyTerms.definition: An interpretation of quantum mechanics on which quantum indeterminism reflects our ignorance of further causal factors, so the underlying dynamics is deterministic.
keyTerms.example: Some cite it to answer the objection that quantum mechanics refutes causality.
keyTerms.origin: Louis de Broglie (1927) and David Bohm (1952).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The Aristotelian reply itself. Feser mentions Bohm but doesn’t rely on it, since causality doesn’t require determinism anyway.

keyTerms.definition: Constraints, derived by John Bell, that any ‘local’ theory of hidden causes must satisfy. Experiments show they are violated, revealing correlations between distant measurements that seem to lack a common cause.
keyTerms.example: Entangled particles measured far apart show correlated results.
keyTerms.origin: Physicist John S. Bell, 1964.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Proof that there is no cause. The violations rule out only certain kinds of cause (local ones), and various causal accounts have been proposed.

keyTerms.definition: The lowest-energy state of a quantum field. It is not empty ‘nothing’ but a physical system with structure, in which particles can briefly appear and disappear.
keyTerms.example: The objection that particles pop into existence at random in the vacuum.
keyTerms.origin: Quantum field theory, 20th-century physics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Absolute nothingness. A vacuum has a definite nature and obeys laws, so particles emerging from it are potentials of a field being actualized.

keyTerms.definition: Heisenberg’s suggestion that the probabilities of quantum theory describe objective tendencies or potentialities, similar to Aristotle’s notion of potency.
keyTerms.example: Heisenberg said physicists came to treat electron orbits not as full reality but as a kind of potentia.
keyTerms.origin: Werner Heisenberg, Physics and Philosophy (1958), borrowing Aristotle’s term.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere ignorance or subjective probability. Heisenberg meant a real, objective tendency in nature.

keyTerms.definition: In comic-book art, a contour that is left out of the black line art and rendered only by the color added later. A careful viewer can still infer it from the lines that are drawn.
keyTerms.example: Feser’s image for quantum theory as line art whose lines hint at the causality they don’t depict.
keyTerms.origin: Comic-art production technique.
keyTerms.confuseWith: An ordinary black-and-white drawing, whose missing color just goes unrecorded. A color hold is designed so that the missing elements can be inferred.

keyTerms.definition: Aquinas’ idea that some activity follows from a substance’s own nature, without a continuously conjoined external mover. Its efficient cause is whatever generated the substance with that nature.
keyTerms.example: A body’s inertial motion, or a lead-210 atom’s tendency to decay, read as flowing from its form.
keyTerms.origin: Thomas Aquinas; the terminology is from James Weisheipl, Nature and Motion in the Middle Ages.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Uncaused motion. ‘Spontaneous’ here means the motion flows from the thing’s nature (its formal cause), with an efficient cause in what generated it.

keyTerms.definition: In Aristotelian physics, the specific location toward which a body naturally tends to move, such as the center of the earth for heavy bodies.
keyTerms.example: The medieval explanation of why a dropped stone falls.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle, Physics and On the Heavens.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Aristotle’s metaphysics of act and potency. Natural place is a refuted scientific thesis, and the argument doesn’t depend on it.

keyTerms.definition: Physicist Arthur Eddington’s contrast between the everyday table (solid, extended, substantial) and the scientific table (a cloud of particles in mostly empty space).
keyTerms.example: An objector uses it to say that ‘the desk holds up the cup’ is scientifically naïve.
keyTerms.origin: Sir Arthur Eddington, The Nature of the Physical World (1928).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A real conflict between physics and common sense. Feser argues the particle story describes the mechanism by which the desk holds the cup.

keyTerms.definition: The philosophical view that the natural world studied by science is all there is, with no supernatural or immaterial reality. A holder of the view is a ‘naturalist’ (not to be confused with a nature-lover).
keyTerms.example: Feser notes naturalists routinely defend causal theories of knowledge, perception and meaning, which commits them to real causation.
keyTerms.origin: A modern philosophical position; it provides the intellectual foundation of much modern atheism.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Science. Naturalism is a philosophical thesis about science’s scope, not a scientific finding.

keyTerms.definition: An endless chain in which each step explains the one before it only by appealing to something that needs the very same explanation, so nothing is ever explained.
keyTerms.example: D is actualized by C only as C is actualized by B, and so on without end: the power to actualize is never accounted for.
keyTerms.origin: Classic philosophical diagnosis, used by Aristotle and Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A harmless (benign) infinite series, such as the natural numbers or a beginningless linear series of begettings, where nothing depends on borrowed power.

keyTerms.definition: Mumford and Anjum’s distinction between causation occurring within a single process and one process merely setting up conditions for a later, separate process.
keyTerms.example: Sugar dissolving in tea sets up conditions for the tea later being drunk; it doesn’t cause the drinking in the way water and sugar’s structure cause the dissolving.
keyTerms.origin: Stephen Mumford and Rani Lill Anjum, Getting Causes from Powers (2011).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A single long simultaneous causal chain. The distinction explains why immediate simultaneity doesn’t collapse all causal history into one instant.

keyTerms.definition: Special relativity’s result that whether two spatially separated events are simultaneous depends on the observer’s frame of reference.
keyTerms.example: Two lightning strikes far apart may be simultaneous for one observer and not for another.
keyTerms.origin: Albert Einstein, special relativity (1905).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The simultaneity of an immediate cause and its effect, which are parts of one event at one place, so relativity doesn’t apply to them.

keyTerms.definition: A hypothetical collection of many universes, of which ours would be one. Some cosmologists speculate that such a collection might have no beginning even if our universe does.
keyTerms.example: The suggestion that our universe branched off from a parallel universe, or arose from an earlier universe collapsing, in a series stretching back forever.
keyTerms.origin: Twentieth-century cosmology and interpretations of quantum mechanics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The universe as usually understood. For the argument it makes no difference, since Feser grants that the universe or a multiverse may have no beginning.

keyTerms.definition: A different first-cause argument: whatever begins to exist has a cause, the universe began to exist, so it has a cause. Unlike the Aristotelian proof, it depends on the universe having a beginning.
keyTerms.example: Arguing from the Big Bang to a cause of the universe’s beginning.
keyTerms.origin: Medieval Islamic theology (kalām, Arabic for ‘speech’ or ‘discourse’), especially al-Ghazali; defended today by William Lane Craig.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The Aristotelian proof, which grants a possibly beginningless universe and concerns what sustains things now.

keyTerms.definition: The actualizing of a thing’s potential at the very same moment the thing has that feature. Concurrent means ‘running together in time’. Sustaining causes act concurrently with their effects.
keyTerms.example: The desk actualizes the cup’s being three feet up at the same moment the cup is three feet up; the atoms’ bonding actualizes the water’s existence right now.
keyTerms.origin: Feser’s formal statement (steps 7 and 10); Latin concurrere, ‘to run together’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Divine ‘concurrence’ in the technical theological sense (God’s cooperation with creatures’ actions), which the chapter on God’s nature discusses separately.

keyTerms.definition: Anything that is partly actual and partly potential, meaning actual in some respects and able to be otherwise in others. Every changeable thing is such a mixture; pure actuality is not.
keyTerms.example: The water is actually water but potentially separate gases; your arm is actually here but potentially there.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian–Thomistic metaphysics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A composite of physical parts. Something could in principle have no physical parts and still mix act and potency; the argument concerns the metaphysical mixture.

keyTerms.definition: The characteristics that belong to God as traditionally conceived. Stage 2 derives unity, immutability, eternity, immateriality, incorporeality, perfection, goodness, omnipotence, intelligence and omniscience.
keyTerms.example: Steps 15–47 of the formal argument, each block deriving one attribute from pure actuality.
keyTerms.origin: Classical philosophical theology (Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas, Maimonides, Avicenna).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Anthropomorphic traits (having a body, emotions, a location). The derived attributes deny limitations rather than attributing human features.

keyTerms.definition: A concept that applies to every possible instance of a kind, not just to this or that particular thing. ‘Abstract’ means drawn off from particular instances; ‘universal’ means applying to all of them.
keyTerms.example: Your concept of man applies to every man who exists, has existed or could exist; your concept of triangle covers triangles of every size and shape.
keyTerms.origin: Latin universalis, ‘pertaining to the whole’; abstractus, ‘drawn away’. Plato and Aristotle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A mental image, which is always particular (a specific size, color or shape). You can’t picture ‘triangle in general’, but you can understand it.

keyTerms.definition: Misrepresenting an opponent’s position as a weaker version and then refuting that weaker version instead of the real one.
keyTerms.example: Attacking the claim ‘everything has a cause’ when the argument actually says ‘whatever goes from potential to actual has a cause’.
keyTerms.origin: An informal fallacy, named after a scarecrow-like figure set up only to be knocked down.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A simplified but fair summary. Simplifying is fine if it keeps the premises the real argument uses.

keyTerms.definition: Describes a claim adopted only to rescue a position from an objection, with no independent motivation.
keyTerms.example: The charge that theists invented the potential-to-actual formulation just to dodge ‘What caused God?’. Feser says the charge is false.
keyTerms.origin: Latin ad hoc, ‘for this (purpose only)’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A principled restriction. A restriction that follows from an independent analysis (here, Aristotle’s analysis of change) isn’t ad hoc, even if it also blocks an objection.

keyTerms.definition: Reasoning to a claim because it explains the evidence better than the alternatives do.
keyTerms.example: Feser argues that the principle of causality best explains why we find causes when we look, and why things don’t pop into existence randomly.
keyTerms.origin: A standard pattern of scientific and philosophical reasoning (C. S. Peirce called it ‘abduction’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Deductive proof. The chapter’s main argument is deductive; this kind of inference appears only as extra support against Hume.

keyTerms.definition: Physics tells us the mathematical structure of events, meaning how measurable quantities relate. It is silent on the intrinsic nature of what has that structure: what it is that changes and what it changes from and to.
keyTerms.example: The later Russell conceded that physics gives only abstract equations, leaving the intrinsic character of events unknown.
keyTerms.origin: Bertrand Russell’s later work (e.g. My Philosophical Development); today’s ‘structural realism’ debates.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The claim that physics is false. The point is that physics is partial: accurate about structure, silent about what bears it.

keyTerms.definition: An objection to an argument showing that, if it worked, it would also establish obviously false conclusions, so something in it must be wrong.
keyTerms.example: If absence from the equations proved causes unreal, it would also prove ‘law’, ‘event’ and ‘variable’ unreal (Schaffer’s point against Russell).
keyTerms.origin: A traditional method of refutation, a form of reductio ad absurdum.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Overstating one’s own conclusion. ‘Proving too much’ is a diagnosis of a flawed argument, not a complaint about exaggeration.

keyTerms.definition: The broad tradition of thought stemming from Aristotle. It includes scientific theses (geocentrism, four elements, natural places), many of them refuted, and metaphysical theses (act and potency, form and matter, the four causes), which Feser argues remain sound.
keyTerms.example: The objection that ‘Aristotelianism was refuted by modern science’ runs the two kinds of thesis together.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle (384–322 BC), carried on by commentators and medieval scholastics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Aristotle’s physics specifically. Rejecting his astronomy doesn’t touch his metaphysics.

keyTerms.definition: The part of philosophy that studies the most general features of reality, such as being, change, causation, substance, act and potency, which any science presupposes.
keyTerms.example: The thesis that change is the actualization of a potential is metaphysical, not scientific, since every observation already presupposes it.
keyTerms.origin: Greek ta meta ta physika, ‘the (books) after the Physics’, the title given to Aristotle’s treatise.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The occult or ‘mystical’, as in bookstore usage; or pure speculation. In philosophy it is the rigorous study of the foundations of reality.

keyTerms.definition: The principle that there is an explanation for why anything exists and has the features it has. It is broader than the principle of causality.
keyTerms.example: The Rationalist proof (Chapter 5) relies on the PSR; the Aristotelian proof needs only the narrower claim that potentials can’t actualize themselves.
keyTerms.origin: Leibniz’s formulation; related ideas in Parmenides, Spinoza and others.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The principle of causality (PC). PC concerns only transitions from potential to actual; PSR concerns everything.

keyTerms.definition: The traditional conception of God as one, simple, immutable, eternal, immaterial, perfect, omnipotent, omniscient and wholly good, the sustaining cause of all things, as found in Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas, Maimonides and Avicenna.
keyTerms.example: The ‘God as traditionally conceived’ whom step 49 identifies with the purely actual cause.
keyTerms.origin: The mainstream of Jewish, Christian and Islamic philosophical theology.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Theistic personalism, which pictures God as a very great person alongside the world, changing and in time. Feser’s argument supports classical theism.

keyTerms.definition: Aristotle’s four kinds of explanation: material (what a thing is made of), formal (its nature or form), efficient (what produces or sustains it) and final (what it is for, or tends toward).
keyTerms.example: In Feser’s analysis, lead-210 decay has a formal cause (its nature) and efficient causes (what generated it and what sustains it).
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle, Physics II and Metaphysics V.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The modern habit of using ‘cause’ to mean only an efficient cause.

keyTerms.definition: An essential feature belongs to something because of what it is; a contingent (or ‘accidental’) feature just happens to be true of it. Confusing the two is the fallacy of accident.
keyTerms.example: Being under seven feet tall is a contingent feature of every U.S. president so far, not essential to being president. Likewise, changing while acting is contingent to the causes we know.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s distinction between essence and accident.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Accidental’ in the everyday sense of ‘by mishap’. Here it simply means ‘not required by the nature of the thing’.

keyTerms.definition: The rigorous philosophical and theological method of the medieval universities (and its modern revivals), which developed Aristotle’s ideas. Much of this chapter’s vocabulary comes from it: per se/per accidens, formally/virtually/eminently, actus purus.
keyTerms.example: Feser’s footnotes point to his book Scholastic Metaphysics for fuller treatment of act and potency and causal series.
keyTerms.origin: Latin scholasticus, ‘of the school’. Aquinas, Scotus and others; revived as ‘Neo-Scholasticism’ and ‘Thomism’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere hair-splitting. The ‘fine distinctions’ scholastics drew, such as per se vs. per accidens, often do real work, as this chapter shows.

distinctions.name: Per accidens vs. per se causal series

left.label: Per accidens (linear, accidentally ordered)
left.desc: Members are strung out in time and each has its own causal power relative to the others; a later member can keep acting after earlier ones disappear (the air conditioner runs after you leave; Bob begets Chuck whether or not Al is alive). Such a series could in principle have no beginning.

right.label: Per se (hierarchical, essentially ordered)
right.desc: Every member but the first has only derived, instrumental power and acts only while being acted on (desk held by floor held by foundation). Remove the source and the whole series stops at once. It must have a first member with underived power — even if it were infinitely long.

distinctions.whyItMatters: This is the hinge of the entire proof. The argument concedes an infinite past and rests everything on the per se series that sustains things in being right now. Most popular objections (‘the universe might be eternal’, ‘why can’t the chain go back forever?’) confuse the two.

distinctions.name: Actuality vs. potentiality

left.label: Actuality
left.desc: What a thing actually is here and now; only the actual can act or cause.

right.label: Potentiality
right.desc: What a thing can become — real but unrealized, determinate (coffee can cool, not turn into soup), and incapable of actualizing itself.

distinctions.whyItMatters: It explains change without Parmenides’ something-from-nothing, grounds the principle of causality, and defines the conclusion (pure actuality) from which every divine attribute is derived.

distinctions.name: ‘First’ in time vs. ‘first’ in the order of dependence

left.label: Temporally first
left.desc: The earliest member of a series, the one at the beginning — e.g., whatever triggered the Big Bang.

right.label: First as primary / underived
right.desc: The member whose causal power is built in rather than borrowed, and on which all the others depend right now for their power to act.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The argument’s First Cause is first in the second sense. That is why the age of the universe, and whether time had a beginning, are irrelevant.

distinctions.name: Cause of coming-to-be vs. cause of being (sustaining cause)

left.label: Cause of becoming
left.desc: What originally produced a thing — the brewing of the coffee, the chemical reaction that bonded hydrogen and oxygen, the parents who begot a child.

right.label: Cause of being
right.desc: What makes the thing exist right now, at this instant — what actualizes the matter’s potential to be water rather than separate gases here and now.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The argument asks the second question. Answers to the first (‘a past process made it’) or about possible destruction (‘nothing has broken it up yet’) don’t touch it.

distinctions.name: ‘Everything has a cause’ vs. ‘whatever goes from potential to actual has a cause’

left.label: The straw man
left.desc: Everything whatsoever has a cause — which would indeed make ‘What caused God?’ a fair question.

right.label: The actual principle
right.desc: Only what passes from potency to act needs an actualizer; what is purely actual has nothing to be actualized, so it neither needs nor could have a cause.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Keeping them apart defuses the most common objection to every first-cause argument. The difference is like that between ‘all triangles have three sides’ and ‘all figures have three sides’.

distinctions.name: Formal vs. virtual vs. eminent possession of an effect

left.label: Formally
left.desc: The cause has the very feature it gives (I hand you a twenty from my wallet).

right.label: Virtually or eminently
right.desc: The cause has the power to obtain it (bank credit) or the higher power to produce such things at all (authority to print money).

distinctions.whyItMatters: Proportionate causality does not mean God must be a cat to cause cats. The forms of things are in God eminently — as ideas in an intellect — which is how Stage 2 derives intelligence and omniscience.

distinctions.name: Absence from the representation vs. representation of absence

left.label: Absent from the representation
left.desc: A black-and-white drawing contains no color; mathematical physics contains no ‘causes’, only equations.

right.label: Represented as absent
right.desc: A claim that the scene itself is colorless, or that nature itself lacks causation.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Russell’s, Newtonian, relativistic and quantum objections all slide from the first to the second. If a method is guaranteed to leave something out, its omission is no evidence the thing is missing.

distinctions.name: Unmoved vs. unmovable

left.label: Unmoved (in fact)
left.desc: A first actualizer that isn’t actually being actualized while it acts, but might still have unrealized potentials.

right.label: Unmovable (purely actual)
right.desc: An actualizer with no potentiality at all, and so incapable of being actualized.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Only the second yields the divine attributes. Feser argues the first is incoherent as a first actualizer of existence: any potential in it would need an actualizer, sending us beyond it or into a vicious regress.

illustrations.title: The cooling cup of coffee
illustrations.body:
Hot coffee on your desk has a real potential to become cold — along with potentials to stain the rug or wake you up — but no potential to become chicken soup or a live chicken. When it cools, that potential is actualized, not by itself (a mere potential can’t do anything) but by the actual coolness of the air or by ice cubes you drop in.

Use it to teach three things at once: change is real, potentiality is something rather than nothing (answering Parmenides), and potentials need actual actualizers (the principle of causality).

illustrations.title: The cup on the desk on the floor on the earth — and the hanging lamp
illustrations.body:
The cup is three feet up because the desk holds it *right now*; the desk holds it only because the floor holds the desk *right now*; and so on to the foundation and the earth. A lamp hangs from a chain, held by a fixture, held by the ceiling, held by walls and foundation. Knock out any lower member and everything above it falls at once.

This is Feser’s model of a **hierarchical** series: every intermediate member is like an instrument with borrowed power. Contrast the air conditioner, which keeps cooling the room after you’ve left the house (a **linear** series).

illustrations.title: The painter, the brush — and the infinitely long handle
illustrations.body:
The painter paints the picture; the brush is merely his instrument. A brush has no power to move itself, and it wouldn’t gain any if its handle were infinitely long. If the brush is moving, something with built-in power to move it must be at work.

This shows why ‘first cause’ doesn’t mean ‘earliest cause’, and why making a hierarchical series infinite doesn’t remove the need for a primary cause: more instruments are still just instruments.

illustrations.title: What keeps the water in the coffee existing?
illustrations.body:
The matter that is now water could exist instead as separate hydrogen and oxygen. What actualizes its potential to be water *at this instant*? ‘A reaction in the past’ tells you how it got here; ‘nothing has split it yet’ tells you how it might stop existing. Chemical bonding just restates the question, and atomic structure pushes it one level down to subatomic particles.

We have a hierarchical series of actualizers of *existence*, which must end in something whose existence needs no actualizing — pure actuality.

illustrations.title: The $20 gift
illustrations.body:
I can give you $20 only if I somehow have it: a twenty in my wallet (formally), money in my bank account (virtually), or even the power to print twenty-dollar bills (eminently). If I have it in none of these ways, I can’t give it.

This illustrates the principle of proportionate causality, which Stage 2 uses to show that the cause of all things must contain their forms — not by *being* a cat or a tree, but eminently, as ideas in an intellect.

illustrations.title: Metal detectors, easy courses, and the drunk under the streetlamp
illustrations.body:
A metal detector’s success doesn’t show there’s no wood or stone in the ground. A student who takes only classes he knows he’ll ace can’t conclude other subjects contain nothing important. A drunk who finds things under the streetlamp can’t infer his keys aren’t somewhere in the dark.

Physics deliberately attends only to what can be mathematized, so its silence about causes, potentials, or intrinsic natures is no evidence against them. Feser uses these analogies against Russell, and again against the inertia and quantum objections.

illustrations.title: The black-and-white drawing and the ‘color hold’
illustrations.body:
A line drawing has no color, but that doesn’t show the scene was colorless — the method just can’t record color. In a ‘color hold’, some contours are left out of the ink and supplied only by the color added later; a sharp viewer can still infer, from the lines that are drawn, where the missing edges of a cube must be.

Physics is the line art; physics plus metaphysics is the finished colored picture. Quantum theory, with what Heisenberg compared to Aristotle’s *potentia*, may be line art whose lines hint at the causality they don’t depict.

illustrations.title: Mirrors all the way down
illustrations.body:
A mirror shows the image of a face that is in another mirror, which shows the image in another, and so on without end. Even if such an infinite hall of mirrors were possible, the image must come from an actual face that isn’t just reflecting something else. You can’t have mirror images with no face.

In the same way, an infinite hierarchy of instrumental causes would still need a source of underived causal power outside the series.

illustrations.title: The movie on the screen
illustrations.body:
The image on a cinema screen exists only as long as the projector is running and its bulb is shining. It doesn’t matter how long the film has been playing or whether it had a ‘first frame’; at every instant, the picture exists only because light is being cast on it *now*. Switch off the bulb and the picture doesn’t fade out over centuries — it vanishes instantly.

This is a good way to convey a per se series of existence: the question is not ‘what started the movie?’ but ‘what is keeping the picture there right now?’ (Where the analogy breaks down: the bulb itself needs power; only something purely actual would be a source that needs no source.)

illustrations.title: A train of boxcars with no engine
illustrations.body:
Each boxcar is pulled by the one in front of it. Add more boxcars — a thousand, a million, infinitely many — and you still have no motion at all unless there is an engine, something that pulls without being pulled. Length doesn’t turn borrowed motion into motion that nobody supplies.

This helps skeptics see why ‘just make the regress infinite’ doesn’t work for instrumental causes. Stress that the engine is ‘first’ by *nature* (it pulls on its own power), not merely by position at the front.

objections.title: A first cause isn’t the God of theism
objections.whoRaises: Typical skeptic; many popular critics of cosmological arguments
objections.objection: Even if the argument gets you to some first cause, it can’t tell you what that cause is like. For all it shows, the cause could be an impersonal force, a quantum field, or a committee of gods. Calling it ‘God’ is a bait-and-switch.
objections.reply:
Feser calls this objection common but entirely ungrounded. The Aristotelian argument doesn’t reach a vague ‘something’; it reaches something **purely actual**, and pure actuality has consequences:

1. No potential means no change: **immutable**.
2. No change means no time: **eternal**.
3. No change or time means no matter: **immaterial, incorporeal**.
4. No unrealized potential means no privation: **perfect** and **fully good**.
5. Nothing to differentiate two such beings: **one**.
6. The source of all actualizing power: **omnipotent**.
7. By proportionate causality, the forms of everything must be in it abstractly: **intelligent** and **omniscient**.

That is the traditional concept of God, and it is derived, not assumed. A fuller defense of each attribute comes in the later chapter on the divine nature.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘those derivations rest on contested assumptions’, agree that they need defending — Feser says so himself — but point out that the objection has now changed. It is no longer ‘a first-cause argument *can’t* tell you anything about the cause’; it’s ‘I dispute step 16 (or 28, or 42)’. That is a specific premise you can examine together. Also note that an impersonal force or quantum field has potentials (it can be in different states), so it can’t be what is purely actual.

objections.title: The universe may not have had a beginning
objections.whoRaises: Readers who assume every theistic argument is a ‘Big Bang’ argument; defenders of eternal or cyclic cosmologies
objections.objection: The argument says that if you trace causes back in time you reach God at the beginning of the universe. But we don’t know the universe had a beginning — the Big Bang might have come from an earlier universe, and an infinite multiverse might have no start at all.
objections.reply: This is a misreading. Feser explicitly **grants**, for argument’s sake, that the universe — or a series of universes — might stretch infinitely into the past. Aristotle himself believed the world was eternal. Whether the cosmos had a beginning is **irrelevant** because the argument concerns a **hierarchical** series of causes that sustain things **here and now**, not a linear series running back through time. Even in a beginningless universe, the water in your coffee exists at this moment only because its potential to exist as water is being actualized at this moment.
objections.pushback: If they still insist ‘but the chain has to go back to God at some point’, draw two diagrams: a horizontal line of events (linear — can be infinite) and a vertical stack of dependencies at a single moment (hierarchical — needs a top). Ask them which one the argument uses. Beginningless-multiverse cosmologies speak only to the horizontal line.

objections.title: Fallacy of composition: the whole universe needn’t have a cause
objections.whoRaises: Bertrand Russell–style critics; introductory philosophy textbooks
objections.objection: Even if every part of the universe has a cause, it doesn’t follow that the universe as a whole has one. Inferring a cause of the whole from causes of the parts is a fallacy of composition.
objections.reply: No premise of the argument is about the universe as a whole. It begins with **any single object existing now** — a stone, a cup of coffee — and shows that for *that one thing* to exist even for a moment, a purely actual cause must be actualizing it at that moment. Feser does go on to say this applies to every material thing, and so to the universe as a whole — but that is a **consequence** drawn from the argument, not a premise it relies on.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘generalizing from the coffee to everything is still composition’, point out that it’s not composition but ordinary universal instantiation: the reasoning applies to *each* thing with a potential for existence, one at a time, because each has that potential. No claim about the whole is inferred from the parts.

objections.title: ‘If everything has a cause, what caused God?’
objections.whoRaises: Popular atheist writers; the most common objection in casual conversation
objections.objection: The argument says everything needs a cause, then exempts God. If God can exist uncaused, why not the universe? This is special pleading.
objections.reply:
Two points.

1. The argument never says ‘everything has a cause’. Its principle is that **whatever goes from potential to actual** needs an actualizer.
2. The exemption is not arbitrary; it follows from the principle’s own rationale. Things need causes *because* they have potentials that must be actualized. What is **purely actual** has no potentials — nothing in it that needs to be, or even could be, actualized. So it is the one thing that neither needs nor could have a cause.

The universe, by contrast, is full of potentiality — it changes constantly — so it is exactly the sort of thing that needs an actualizer.
