options: Images are illusions
Even an infinite series of derivative items needs an underived source outside it
Mirrors are instrumental causes of faces
Actual infinities are impossible
quiz.explanation: However many mirrors there are, there must be an actual face supplying the image. Feser doesn’t argue that infinity is impossible (D); he argues that derived content needs an underived source.

quiz.q: In the Al–Bob–Chuck footnote, what is the MOST important sense, according to Feser, in which none of them has inherent causal power ‘full stop’?
options: Each inherited the power to beget from his parents
Each will eventually die
Each came into existence at a particular time
None could act at all unless the matter of his body were being actualized here and now
quiz.explanation: Feser mentions inheritance (A) as one sense but says the most important is dependence on present hierarchical series. That is why every stage of a linear series presupposes hierarchical ones.

quiz.q: Someone says, “God is the biggest, most powerful thing in the universe.” Which correction follows from the chapter?
options: God is not one actual thing among others but pure actuality: immaterial, one, and outside time
God is the size of the whole universe
God is infinitely extended matter
God is the first event in the history of the cosmos
quiz.explanation: Pure actuality is immaterial and eternal, so it isn’t a ‘thing in the universe’ at all, however large. It is the source of all actuality, not a member of the series.

quiz.q: To deny divine unity, which step would a critic most directly have to reject?
options: Step 1
Step 38
Step 16
Step 49
quiz.explanation: Step 16 claims a differentiating feature would require an unactualized potential. Reject it and two purely actual beings might be distinguishable. Step 38 concerns intelligence, not unity.

shortAnswer.q: Explain how Aristotle’s distinction between actuality and potentiality answers Parmenides’ argument against change.
shortAnswer.model: Parmenides argued that change would require something to come from nothing — the coffee’s coldness doesn’t exist while it is hot, so if the coffee cools, coldness arises from nothing, which is impossible. Aristotle replies that the coldness wasn’t simply nothing: it existed **potentially**. The coffee has a real, determinate capacity to become cold (unlike a capacity to become chicken soup). Change is the **actualization** of such a potential, so nothing comes from sheer nothingness. Feser also notes that denying change is self-refuting, since reasoning is itself a change.
rubric: States Parmenides’ something-from-nothing argument
Defines potentiality as real but unactualized, not nothing
Uses an example showing potentials are determinate (can/can’t become)
Defines change as actualization of potential

shortAnswer.q: Why does the principle of causality follow from the nature of potentiality rather than being a mere generalization from experience?
shortAnswer.model: A potential is, by definition, not yet actual. What is not actual can’t do anything — only what actually exists can act. So a potential can’t make itself actual: if it could, it would already have to be actual, which contradicts its being merely potential. Therefore every actualization requires something already actual. Experience confirms this abundantly, but the principle rests on what potentiality is, which is why it can be applied beyond experience (Feser’s reply to Kant).
rubric: Potential = not yet actual
Only the actual can act/cause
So no potential actualizes itself
Notes this grounds the principle’s generality beyond observed cases

shortAnswer.q: Distinguish linear and hierarchical causal series, giving an example of each, and explain why only the hierarchical kind must have a first member.
shortAnswer.model: In a **linear (per accidens)** series, each member has its own causal power relative to the others and can keep acting after earlier members are gone — the air conditioner keeps cooling after you leave; Bob begets Chuck whether or not Al is alive. Nothing in such a series requires tracing any member’s activity back to a first, so it could be beginningless. In a **hierarchical (per se)** series, every member except the first has only borrowed, instrumental power and acts only while being acted on — the desk holds the cup only while the floor holds the desk. Borrowed power must come from something that has it unborrowed; otherwise nothing in the series could act at all. Even an infinite series of instruments (an infinitely long brush handle) would need a primary cause.
rubric: Correct linear example and characterization (inherent power, can outlast predecessors)
Correct hierarchical example and characterization (derived/instrumental power, concurrent dependence)
Explains that linear series need no first member
Explains that borrowed power requires an underived source regardless of length

shortAnswer.q: Explain the move from the changes a thing undergoes to the thing’s existence at a moment. Why is this move so important?
shortAnswer.model: Change presupposes a thing that changes: coffee can cool only if it exists. So Feser asks what keeps the coffee — or its water — in existence right now. The water’s matter could exist as separate hydrogen and oxygen; its being water now is an actualized potential. Past causes explain how it came to be, and the absence of disruptors explains how it might cease, but neither explains what makes it water now. Chemical bonds and atomic structure only push the question down a level. This reveals a hierarchical series of actualizers of existence. The move matters because it makes the argument independent of time: it doesn’t depend on a beginning of the universe, on the timing of causes, or even on the reality of change in the physical world (e.g., the block universe).
rubric: Change presupposes an existing substance
Existence now is an actualized potential (water vs. separate gases)
Distinguishes cause of becoming / ceasing from cause of being now
Identifies a hierarchical series of existence
Explains why this shields the argument from beginning/timing/block-universe objections

shortAnswer.q: Why must the first actualizer be purely actual — unmovable, not just unmoved?
shortAnswer.model: The first actualizer is first because it actualizes others’ existence without its own existence being actualized. If it had any potential needing actualization in order to exist, something would have to actualize it: (1) something else — then it isn’t first; (2) a purely actual part of itself — then that part is the real first actualizer and the potential part is merely its first effect; or (3) a part that is itself mixed act and potency — which would need its own actualizer, restarting a vicious regress. So any genuine first actualizer of existence must be purely actual, and hence has all the attributes that follow from pure actuality.
rubric: Frames the issue as the actualization of existence
Presents the three-way dilemma accurately
Explains why each horn fails
Draws the conclusion that a first actualizer must be pure act

shortAnswer.q: Derive the attributes of immutability, eternity and immateriality from pure actuality.
shortAnswer.model: Change is the actualization of potential; what is purely actual has no potential, so it can’t change — it is **immutable**. Existing in time entails changeability (succession, before and after), so an immutable being isn’t in time — it is **eternal** in the sense of timeless, without beginning, end or succession. Being material entails changeability and temporality, so what is immutable and eternal is **immaterial**, and so also **incorporeal**, having no body.
rubric: Immutability from no potential + definition of change
Eternity as timelessness from immutability
Immateriality from matter entailing change and time
Incorporeality from immateriality

shortAnswer.q: Explain the principle of proportionate causality, using the $20 example, and show how Stage 2 uses it to establish divine intelligence.
shortAnswer.model: What is in an effect must be in its cause somehow, since a cause can’t give what it lacks. I can give you $20 only if I have it **formally** (a twenty in my wallet), **virtually** (credit in the bank I can draw on), or **eminently** (the higher power to print twenties). The purely actual cause is the cause of everything that exists or could exist; to cause a thing is to cause something of a particular form (a cat, a tree). So the forms of all things must be in the cause — not formally (it isn’t a cat) but eminently, and in a universal, abstract way, since it causes every possible instance. Having forms abstractly without being those things is exactly what intellect is. Since it also causes the relations among things (this cat on this mat), these pre-exist in it as combinations of forms, like thoughts or a craftsman’s plans. So it is intelligent — and, since nothing lies outside its thoughts, omniscient.
rubric: States the principle (cause can’t give what it doesn’t have)
Correctly explains formally/virtually/eminently with the $20 cases
Cause of everything → forms of everything in it
Forms present abstractly/universally = intellect
Notes omniscience follows

shortAnswer.q: What is wrong with the objection ‘If everything has a cause, what caused God?’ Include Feser’s response to the charge that the argument’s formulation is ad hoc.
shortAnswer.model: The argument never says everything has a cause; it says whatever goes from potential to actual has a cause. That difference is like the difference between ‘all triangles have three sides’ and ‘all figures have three sides’. And the exemption for God isn’t arbitrary: things need causes because they have potentials, and pure actuality has none, so it neither needs nor could have a cause. Against the ad hoc charge: (1) motives don’t refute arguments (that would be ad hominem); (2) historically, Aristotelians from Aristotle through Aquinas to today have always stated the principle this way; (3) it follows naturally from the analysis of change, independent of theism.
rubric: Correct statement of the real principle
Explains why the exemption follows from the principle’s rationale
Mentions the triangle analogy or equivalent
Gives the three replies to the ad hoc charge

shortAnswer.q: Summarize Feser’s general strategy for answering objections from physics (Russell, inertia, relativity, quantum mechanics).
shortAnswer.model: Mathematical physics deliberately confines itself to what can be described mathematically — a ‘partial consideration’ of nature. That is the source of its predictive success, but it guarantees physics will omit qualitative and causal features such as potentiality. So **absence from the representation is not a representation of absence** (a black-and-white drawing doesn’t show a colorless scene; a metal detector doesn’t show there’s no wood). Moreover, laws of physics describe how things with certain natures behave, so they presuppose the existence of such things and can’t explain what sustains them. Science also presupposes change in the scientist’s experience. Hence these objections affect at most how the principle of causality applies, not whether it does. Specific points: causation isn’t determinism (quantum); the block universe’s existence would still need an actualizer; inertia is assumed by mathematical physics, not proved.
rubric: Physics as mathematical abstraction / partial consideration
Absence from representation ≠ representation of absence (with an analogy)
Laws presuppose natures and existing things
Science presupposes change in experience
At least two specific applications (quantum determinism, block universe, inertia, Russell)

shortAnswer.q: How does Feser defend the reality of hierarchical causal series against the objection that there are no truly simultaneous causes?
shortAnswer.model: First, simultaneous doesn’t mean instantaneous: a cause’s acting and the effect’s being acted on are one event, however long it lasts (pushing a chair). Second, immediate causes are always simultaneous with their effects: it is the billiard ball’s impact, not its earlier motion, and the brick’s pressing into the glass, not the throw, that immediately causes the effect (Mumford and Anjum). Third, this doesn’t collapse all causal chains into one instant, because we must distinguish causation within a process from one process setting up conditions for another (sugar dissolving, tea drunk, tea digested). Fourth, relativity of simultaneity concerns separate events at different places, not a cause and effect that are parts of one event at one place. Finally, simultaneity isn’t what makes a series hierarchical anyway — derivative power is — and the key series concerns existence at an instant.
rubric: Simultaneous ≠ instantaneous
Immediate causes simultaneous with effects (an example)
Within-process vs. condition-setting distinction
Relativity irrelevant (same event, same place)
Hierarchy defined by derivative power / existence at an instant

shortAnswer.q: Present Feser’s three replies to Hume’s claim that something could begin to exist without a cause.
shortAnswer.model: (1) Hume only shows we can imagine a thing appearing **without also imagining its cause**, not that we can conceive of it **having no cause**. Conceiving of A without B is not conceiving of A existing without B: a trilateral can be thought of without thinking ‘triangle’, and a man without his height, but neither can exist that way. (2) Following **Anscombe**, Hume must say why the scenario is a case of coming into existence rather than transport from elsewhere, and only the kind of cause marks that difference, so causation re-enters. (3) The principle is **massively confirmed by experience**. We find causes when we look and reasonably assume them when we can’t (unsolved crimes). If it were false, anything could pop up anywhere (Clarke’s elephant or hotel), and constantly. The best explanation is that potentiality by nature needs an actualizer.
rubric: Distinguishes conceiving without a cause from conceiving no cause, with an analogy
States Anscombe’s coming-into-existence vs. transport point
Gives the empirical argument (causes found; things don’t randomly appear)
Draws the inference to the best explanation

shortAnswer.q: Explain the argument for divine unity (steps 15–18) and why material and temporal differences are not available to distinguish purely actual beings.
shortAnswer.model: Two things of a kind can be two only if something distinguishes them, some feature one has that the other lacks. Ordinarily we distinguish things by material or temporal features (larger, taller, here vs. there, earlier vs. later), but pure actuality is immaterial and eternal, so none of those apply. More generally, things of a kind differ by some perfection or privation one has and the other lacks (sturdier roots, a missing tail). But any such difference would mean one of them lacks some actuality, which is an unrealized potential, and pure act has none. So nothing could differentiate two purely actual beings, and there is exactly one.
rubric: States the need for a differentiating feature
Explains why material/temporal features are ruled out (immaterial, eternal)
Explains why perfection/privation differences imply potentiality
Concludes uniqueness

shortAnswer.q: How does Feser respond to the claim that Einstein’s block universe shows change is an illusion?
shortAnswer.model: He doesn’t need to settle whether the block interpretation is correct (it is controversial). (1) Denying all change is **incoherent**: physics rests on observation and experiment, making predictions and then testing them, going from ignorance to knowledge, all of which is change (Richard Healey). At most one could say change exists only in the mind, but change in the mind is still actualization of potential, enough to start the argument. (2) Even with no change anywhere, a thing’s very **existence** involves actualized potential, so the block universe as a whole would still need an actualizer distinct from it, a cause of this world rather than another being actual. So relativity affects how, not whether, the principle of causality applies.
rubric: Describes the block-universe objection accurately
Gives the self-undermining / evidence point
Notes that change in the mind suffices
Gives the existence-of-the-block point
Concludes ‘how, not whether’

shortAnswer.q: Analyze radioactive decay (e.g., lead-210) in Aristotelian terms, as Feser does, and explain why it doesn’t refute the principle of causality.
shortAnswer.model: Lead-210 behaves according to its **nature or form**, as copper conducts electricity and dogs chase squirrels. Its nature includes a probability *x* of decaying in the next minute. So the decay is **indeterministic but intelligible**, grounded in what lead-210 is (its **formal cause**). It also has an **efficient cause** in whatever generated the atom, and, most importantly, a deeper efficient cause in whatever keeps it existing **now** as lead-210 rather than something else or nothing. That actualized potential still needs a purely actual actualizer. Dowe adds that indeterministic links still ground responsibility (the bucket of lead-210) and that scientists call decay the ‘production’ of mercury-206. The objection only works if we conflate causation with deterministic causation.
rubric: Nature/form grounds the probability (formal cause)
Distinguishes intelligibility from determinism
Names the generating efficient cause and the sustaining cause
Uses at least one of Dowe’s points (bucket, ‘production’)

shortAnswer.q: Why can a hierarchical series not be infinite, even though Aristotelians accept infinite mathematical series and possibly beginningless linear series? Include the two objections Feser rebuts here.
shortAnswer.model: In a linear series each member has causal power inherently relative to the others (Bob begets Chuck whether or not Al is alive), so nothing requires tracing activity back to a first member. In a hierarchical series each member acts only by power imparted from outside, so without a member with **underived** power we just pass the explanatory buck. An instrument must be the instrument of something, and length is irrelevant: an infinitely long brush handle still can’t move itself, and endless mirrors still need a real face. **Oppy’s** appeal to infinite mathematical series fails because such series involve no instrumental and primary causes, indeed no causation. **Sobel’s** charge of begging the question fails because calling a cause ‘instrumental’ says only that its power is derived. Whether a regress of derived powers must end is argued, not assumed; even a skeptic sees a stick can’t move a stone on its own.
rubric: Contrasts inherent (linear) vs. derived (hierarchical) power
Explains buck-passing / instrument of nothing, with brush or mirrors
Rebuts the mathematical-series objection
Rebuts the begging-the-question objection

shortAnswer.q: Why does Feser deny that the Aristotelian argument rests on outdated science? Address both the sweeping version and the Eddington version of the objection.
shortAnswer.model: **Sweeping version:** ‘Aristotelianism’ labels a huge range of ideas. Specific scientific theses (geocentrism, the four elements, natural places) were refuted, but the metaphysical thesis that change is actualization of potential was not. Science actually presupposes it, since observation involves passing from one experience to another. The book’s arguments rest on these deeper metaphysical foundations. **Eddington version:** the claim that a desk is really a particle cloud doesn’t conflict with its holding up the cup; it gives the mechanism. The objection is raised selectively (engineers and doctors aren’t accused of outdated science), and the details are irrelevant anyway, since the examples only introduce concepts (actualization, linear vs. hierarchical) that apply at any level of description, affecting how, not whether, they apply. Compare how no one faults a physicist’s ride-a-light-beam thought experiment.
rubric: Separates refuted scientific theses from the metaphysical thesis
Notes that science presupposes change/actualization
Mechanism vs. competition point on Eddington
Selectivity point
Irrelevance point (how, not whether)

flashcards.front: What is change, on Aristotle’s analysis?
flashcards.back: The actualization of a potential — something potentially F becoming actually F.

flashcards.front: Four kinds of change (with Feser’s examples)
flashcards.back: Qualitative (coffee cools), local (leaf falls), quantitative (puddle grows), substantial (swatted fly dies).
Change would require something (e.g. coldness) to come from nothing, which is impossible; so change can’t occur.
(1) Self-refuting: reasoning to the conclusion is itself change. (2) Aristotle: what comes to be was there potentially, and potentiality isn’t nothing.
It’s determinate: coffee can become cold or stain the rug, but not chicken soup or a live chicken.
Any potential that is actualized is actualized by something already actual. (NOT ‘everything has a cause’.)

flashcards.front: Why can’t a potential actualize itself?
flashcards.back: Because what is merely potential isn’t actual, and only what is actual can do anything.

flashcards.front: Does every changer have to be changing?
flashcards.back: No. Only: IF a changer is itself changing, its change needs a changer too.
Members extended in time, each with its own power relative to the others; e.g. button → AC → cool air → cold coffee; Al → Bob → Chuck. Could lack a beginning.
Every member but the first has only derived, instrumental power and acts only while acted on; e.g. earth → foundation → floor → desk → cup. Must have a first member.

flashcards.front: What does ‘first’ mean in ‘first cause’ here?
flashcards.back: Having underived, built-in (primary) causal power — not earliest in time, nor first in a finite list.
It still couldn’t move itself: adding instruments never yields underived power. Length is irrelevant.
AC keeps cooling after you leave (linear: own power). If the floor collapses, desk and cup fall at once (hierarchical: borrowed power).

flashcards.front: Why is the hierarchical series ‘more fundamental’?
flashcards.back: Things can change only if they exist, and their existence at each moment depends on a hierarchical series of actualizers.

flashcards.front: What keeps the water in the coffee existing now?
flashcards.back: Not past causes (how it got here) nor lack of disruptors (how it might cease), but a concurrent actualizer of its matter’s potential to be water — via atoms, particles … ultimately pure actuality.
Feser’s precise name for the Unmoved Mover: something that actualizes other things without being actualized — pure actuality.

flashcards.front: Does the argument need a beginning of the universe?
flashcards.back: No. Feser grants a possibly infinite past (as Aristotle believed); the argument is about sustaining causes now.

flashcards.front: Does the argument assume the universe as a whole has a cause?
flashcards.back: No. It starts from any single thing; applying it to everything is a consequence, not a premise.
Only what goes from potential to actual needs a cause; pure act has no potential, so it neither needs nor could have a cause.
Saying ‘whatever goes from potency to act has a cause’ = ‘everything has a cause’ is like equating ‘all triangles have 3 sides’ with ‘all figures have 3 sides’.

flashcards.front: Three replies to the ‘ad hoc’ charge
flashcards.back: (1) Ad hominem; (2) historically false — always stated this way since Aristotle; (3) follows naturally from the analysis of change.
Conceiving A without conceiving B ≠ conceiving A existing without B (trilateral/triangle; a man without height).
What makes a sudden appearance a coming-into-existence rather than transportation? Only the kind of cause — so causation sneaks back in.
If the principle of causality were false, anything could pop into existence anywhere at any time — but it doesn’t.
We learn geometry from black-ink diagrams but it applies to any color; likewise causality applies wherever there’s potential, observable or not.
Proves too much (Schaffer’s ‘variable’); particles have dispositions (Martin); other sciences and naturalism use causation; physics isn’t exhaustive (later Russell).

flashcards.front: Metal detector / student / drunk under streetlamp
flashcards.back: A method’s success with what it’s built to find tells us nothing about what it can’t detect — physics and causation.
Concerns temporal events, not existence; laws presuppose natures; mathematical physics assumes inertia and abstracts from causes (Weisheipl).

flashcards.front: Two replies on the block universe
flashcards.back: (1) Denying all change is incoherent — science rests on changing experiences (Healey). (2) The block’s very existence would still need an actualizer.
A cause must make its effect intelligible, not necessary. Indeterministic causation is still causation.
Absence from a representation isn’t representation of absence; line art may even hint at what color will supply — like quantum ‘potentia’ (Heisenberg).
Quantum: potentiality without actuality (no actualizer depicted). Block: actuality without potentiality. Both omit causation by method.
Formal (its nature, grounding probability x); efficient (what generated it); deeper efficient (what keeps it in existence now).
If indeterministic links weren’t causal, I wouldn’t be responsible for your radiation sickness — absurd.
Whatever is in an effect is in its cause formally, virtually, or eminently; a cause can’t give what it lacks.
Twenty in the wallet / credit in the bank / power to print twenties.
Grasping universal concepts; combining them into thoughts; reasoning from thought to thought. The first is fundamental.

flashcards.front: Why only one purely actual being?
flashcards.back: Differentiation needs some feature/privation one lacks — i.e., unactualized potential — which pure act can’t have.

flashcards.front: Unmoved vs. unmovable: the three-way dilemma
flashcards.back: A potential in the first actualizer would be actualized by (1) something else — not first; (2) a purely actual part — that part is first; (3) a mixed part — vicious regress.
Inferring all actualizers must change because observed ones do — like concluding no seven-footer could be president.

flashcards.front: What does step 1 claim, and how is it defended?
flashcards.back: Change is real. The senses show it, and even denying it involves a change of mind (Parmenides can’t coherently be believed).
The principle of causality: no potential is actualized except by something already actual.
Any change presupposes a substance that undergoes it; there’s no cooling without something that cools.

flashcards.front: What does step 7 claim and why?
flashcards.back: A substance’s existence at any moment requires its potential for existence to be actualized at that moment. Its matter could be otherwise (water could be separate gases).

flashcards.front: Steps 9–10: the two options for the actualizer A
flashcards.back: Either A’s own existence is being actualized (starting a regress of concurrent actualizers) or A is purely actual.

flashcards.front: What does step 11 claim and why?
flashcards.back: A regress of concurrent actualizers is hierarchical and can’t be infinite, because borrowed power needs an unborrowed source.
There is a purely actual actualizer. This ends Stage 1.
A differentiating feature would require an unactualized potential, which pure act lacks, so there is only one.
Whatever exists in time can change; pure act can’t change; so it exists outside time (eternal).
Matter entails change and time, so pure act is immaterial and therefore incorporeal.
Every actualization comes from pure act directly or via a series ending in it, so all power derives from it (omnipotence).
Forms exist either concretely (in things) or abstractly (in an intellect); they can’t be in pure act concretely, so they’re there as in an intellect.
For there to be a single purely actual cause with these attributes just is for God to exist.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘A first cause isn’t God’ → reply
flashcards.back: Stage 2 derives the divine attributes from pure actuality; the argument goes far beyond a bare cause.
No premise concerns the universe as a whole; the argument starts from any single thing.
Particles are the mechanism of support, not a refutation; the objection is selective, and the details are irrelevant to the concepts.
Simultaneous ≠ instantaneous; immediate causes are one event with their effects; relativity concerns distant events; derivative power is what matters.
They involve no instrumental and primary causes. Aristotelians reject only an infinite series of instruments with no source.
Instrumental means only ‘derives its power from another’; that the regress must end is argued, not assumed.

flashcards.front: Objection: a purely actual actualizer is incoherent → reply
flashcards.back: It begs the question, commits a fallacy of accident (seven-foot president), and isn’t contradictory like ‘immortal mortal’.
Causal accounts exist (faster-than-light influence, backward causation, absolute frame, a law), and physics’ silence isn’t evidence of no cause.
Refuted theses (geocentrism, natural place) are scientific; act and potency is metaphysical, and science presupposes it.

flashcards.front: Distinction: cause of becoming vs. cause of being
flashcards.back: Becoming = what originally produced a thing (brewing). Being = what keeps it existing now. The argument concerns being.
Privation = lacking what one’s nature requires (a blind dog). Negation = lacking what isn’t proper to one (a stone’s lack of sight).
Pure act is uncaused (nothing in it to actualize), not self-caused, which would require existing before itself.
Prime matter depends on form and form on matter, so the composite would be an explanatory circle unless something outside it actualizes it.

flashcards.front: Why the air stays cool after the AC is off
flashcards.back: Members of a linear series have their own causal power, and the cooled air can still chill the coffee for a while.

flashcards.front: Why ‘chemical bonding’ doesn’t answer what keeps water in existence
flashcards.back: It just restates the question: the atoms could be bonded otherwise, so why this way, now? Atomic structure only pushes the question down a level.

teachBack:
**Your challenge:** Explain the Aristotelian proof, out loud, to a smart friend who has never studied philosophy and who believes the universe may be eternal. You have **ten minutes** and one sheet of paper.

**Constraints:**

- You may not say ‘everything has a cause’ or mention the Big Bang except to set it aside.
- You must use one hierarchical example (the cup on the desk, or your own) and one linear example, and say clearly why only one needs a first member.
- You must make the move from change to existence using the water example (water → molecules → atoms → particles).
- You must derive at least **four** divine attributes from pure actuality, including **unity** and **intelligence**.
- Before you finish, invite your friend to ask ‘What caused God?’ and answer it in under 30 seconds.

**Check yourself afterward:**

1. Could your friend repeat, in their own words, the difference between a linear and a hierarchical series?
2. Did you explain *why* a hierarchical series can’t regress infinitely (borrowed power), rather than just asserting it?
3. Did you distinguish ‘first in time’ from ‘first as underived’?
4. Did you avoid overclaiming? (Stage 2 is a sketch; Feser defends the attributes fully later.)
5. Where did you hesitate or reach for jargon? Those are the places to reread — usually the principle of proportionate causality and the unmovable-mover dilemma.

Then repeat the exercise in **three minutes**, and finally in **one sentence**.
videoPrompt: Audience: curious, intelligent adults with no philosophy background, including skeptics. Explain Edward Feser’s Aristotelian proof of God (Chapter 1 of Five Proofs). Emphasize, in order: (1) change is undeniable and means potential becoming actual (hot coffee can become cold, not chicken soup); (2) no potential actualizes itself; (3) the argument is NOT about the Big Bang — grant an eternal universe; (4) linear series (air conditioner keeps running after you leave) vs. hierarchical series (cup held by desk held by floor); (5) what keeps water existing right now — molecules, atoms, particles — must end in pure actuality; (6) why ‘first’ means underived, not earliest (infinitely long paintbrush, mirrors with no face); (7) how unity, immutability, eternity, perfection, omnipotence and intelligence follow. Correct these misconceptions: ‘everything has a cause’, ‘what caused God?’, ‘quantum mechanics shows causeless events’. Tone: clear, warm, rigorous, respectful of skeptics, never preachy.
